format_metric <- function(label, percent = TRUE, digits = 1L) {
  z <- audit[audit$quantity == label, c("panel", "estimate")]
  z$panel <- sub("df_qlfs_", "Panel ", z$panel, fixed = TRUE)
  if (percent) z$estimate <- 100 * z$estimate
  setNames(as.list(round(z$estimate[match(c("Panel A", "Panel B", "Panel C"),
                                         z$panel)], digits)),
           c("Panel A", "Panel B", "Panel C"))
}

# Purpose and status

This document is a reproducible audit and development log for improvements to
the tenure-contamination models reported in Table 7. It is deliberately
separate from the branch-wide summaries. Its purposes are to:

1. document the provenance and construction of the duration variables;
2. record descriptive evidence used to select measurement assumptions;
3. distinguish observed evidence from latent-model interpretation;
4. list every new estimation script and the checks applied to it; and
5. preserve point estimates, diagnostics, and model comparisons as the model
   is extended incrementally.

The start-date audit, job-reset extension, and discrete-month likelihood repair
are implemented and estimated separately from Table 7. The continuous-density
version fails full-model recovery and is retained only as a diagnostic. The
monthly probability-mass version passes repeated recovery checks, converges
from dispersed starts, has regular local inference, and remains stable under
stricter matching panels. It is the current candidate model, but the remaining
measurement-process extensions below should be assessed before it replaces the
paper's Table 7 specification.

# 1. Variable provenance and reconstruction

The upstream mapped QLFS file contains `yearstart` (year commenced working),
`monthstart` (month commenced working), survey `year`, quarterly `wave`, and
the derived tenure variable `timeago`. The matched panels retain `period` and
`tenure`, but not the start-year and start-month components.

For survey period (p), define the nominal interview year and month by

\[
Y(p)=2008+\left\lfloor\frac{p-1}{4}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
M(p)=3\{(p-1)\bmod 4+1\}.
\]

Thus the nominal interview months are March, June, September, and December.
For every upstream record with valid start-year and start-month fields,

\[
\text{tenure months}
=12\{Y(p)-Y^{start}\}+M(p)-M^{start}.
\]

Consequently, the reported start month can be recovered without an upstream
merge as

\[
R_{it}=12Y(p_{it})+M(p_{it})-g_{it},
\]

where (g_{it}) is tenure in months. This is a reported current-job start
month, not necessarily the date of the worker's most recent entry into
employment. The exact interview day is unavailable.

## Audit cautions

- A changed start date may reflect a new job, inconsistent reporting, or an
  incorrect record link.
- A date strictly after the previous nominal interview is strong evidence of
  a job change, but dates in the previous interview month are ambiguous because
  interview days are unavailable.
- The matching algorithms affect which records are linked. Comparisons across
  panels A, B, and C are therefore essential.
- January concentration can reflect genuine seasonality, rounding, or a
  reporting/coding convention. The available labels do not identify which.

# 2. Descriptive start-date audit

The audit uses the paper's age range (18--55), all available consecutive waves,
survey weights, and the three alternative matching panels. It classifies each
consecutive employed pair as an unchanged start date, a plausible job reset, an
ambiguous boundary-month reset, or a revision to a date that predates the
previous interview.

```{r headline-table, results='asis'}
metrics <- list(
  c("Same reported start month", "Same reported start month"),
  c("Plausible job-to-job reset", "Plausible job-to-job reset"),
  c("Boundary-month reset", "Boundary-month reset"),
  c("Any revised pre-existing start date", "Revised pre-existing date"),
  c("Revisions that are exact whole-year shifts", "Whole-year shift among revisions"),
  c("Revised date repeated in the next employed wave", "Revised date repeated next wave"),
  c("Plausible reset repeated in the next employed wave", "Plausible reset repeated next wave"),
  c("January share of reported start months", "Reported start month is January")
)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(metrics, function(m) {
  values <- if (m[1] == "Boundary-month reset") {
    # This measure is stored in the pair-category output, not the summary.
    vapply(c("A", "B", "C"), function(p) {
      f <- file.path(audit_root, paste0("df_qlfs_", p),
                     "consecutive_employed_pair_categories.csv")
      z <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
      100 * z$weighted_share[z$pair == "All" &
        z$category == "Boundary-month reset"]
    }, numeric(1))
  } else {
    unlist(format_metric(m[1]))
  }
  data.frame(Measure = m[2], `Panel A` = values[1], `Panel B` = values[2],
             `Panel C` = values[3], check.names = FALSE)
}))
rownames(tab) <- NULL
knitr::kable(tab, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 1,
             caption = "Start-date audit: survey-weighted percentages",
             linesep = "", longtable = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
             table.envir = "table", position = "H")
```

```{r audit-figure, fig.cap='Reported current-job start dates and their revisions, matching panel A.', out.width='100%', fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(audit_root, "df_qlfs_A",
                                  "job_start_date_audit.png"))
```

## Interpretation

- Most consecutive employed reports preserve exactly the same implied start
  month, and an unchanged date is repeated at the following employed wave in
  roughly nine out of ten cases.
- Stricter matching increases the unchanged share and reduces revisions, so
  matching quality contributes to the observed inconsistencies.
- Large revisions remain common under panel C. They should not be attributed
  exclusively to either respondent reporting or record linkage.
- Exact whole-year shifts and the January concentration favor a calendar-date
  reporting model over a smooth local-error distribution for calculated
  tenure.
- A non-negligible group has a reported job start after the previous interview.
  Current-job tenure can therefore reset without an intervening observed
  nonemployment state.

# 3. Audit of the existing Table 7 likelihood

The preferred current specification combines piecewise duration-dependent
entry and exit hazards, symmetric employment-status misclassification, gross
marginal tenure contamination, and joint per-wave marginal timegap
contamination. Its central duration restriction is that uncontaminated reports
must follow the deterministic clock implied by a latent employment or
nonemployment spell.

For tenure, this treats a maximal latent employment spell as one current-job
spell. That assumption is too strong when a worker can move directly between
jobs. A legitimate job-start reset is then forced into one of three incorrect
interpretations: a contaminated tenure report, a misclassified employment
state, or a latent exit and re-entry.

The local-plus-gross tenure extension does not repair this problem. Its local
component assigns independent bounded deviations around a single employment
clock; it does not allow the underlying current-job clock itself to restart.

# 4. First improved model: a job-change mixture

## Minimal defensible extension

For a latent employed-to-employed transition, introduce a job-continuity event
(J_{it}):

\[
J_{it}=0 \quad\text{same current job},
\qquad
J_{it}=1 \quad\text{new job while remaining employed}.
\]

Let

\[
P(J_{it}=1\mid H_{i,t-1}=H_{it}=1)=q.
\]

Conditional on (J_{it}=0), the uncontaminated tenure clock advances by the
quarterly interval. Conditional on (J_{it}=1), the current-job tenure clock
restarts within the interval. Initially, conditional event time can be taken
as uniform within the quarter; a continuous-time job-change hazard can replace
this approximation later.

This adds only one parameter, (q), and leaves unchanged:

- the latent employment-status transition process;
- employment-status misclassification;
- the piecewise exit and entry hazards;
- tenure-report contamination; and
- timegap contamination.

It is preferable to deterministically splitting spells whenever a date resets.
The mixture allows the likelihood to weigh job change against reporting/linking
inconsistency and remains coherent when reported employment status is itself
misclassified.

## Identification and required comparisons

The job-change probability is identified primarily by short destination tenure
within a latent employed-to-employed transition and by subsequent persistence
of the new start date. The first estimates must be compared on the same sample:

1. current preferred piecewise model;
2. preferred model plus (q);
3. model 2 with (q=0), verifying exact likelihood nesting; and
4. panels A, B, and C, verifying sensitivity to matching quality.

The estimate should not be interpreted as a pure job-to-job transition rate
until identification simulations show that it can be separated from tenure
contamination and status misclassification.

## First estimates

The joint maximum-likelihood fit converged. It estimates a quarterly
employed-to-employed current-job reset probability of
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * job_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`%, and the
survey-weighted posterior mean reset probability is
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * job_comparison$posterior_job_change_rate[2])`%.
The near equality of these two quantities is an internal consistency check.

```{r job-change-comparison}
shown <- job_comparison[, c("model", "loglik", "AIC", "job_change_prob",
  "status_misclassification", "tenure_contamination",
  "timegap_contamination", "weighted_entry", "weighted_exit")]
names(shown) <- c("Model", "Log likelihood", "AIC", "Job reset",
  "Status error", "Tenure error", "Timegap error", "Entry", "Exit")
shown[, 4:9] <- lapply(shown[, 4:9], function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x))
shown[, 2:3] <- lapply(shown[, 2:3], function(x) format(round(x, 1),
  big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))
knitr::kable(shown, booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Preferred duration model and the one-parameter job-change extension")
```

The log likelihood rises by
`r format(round(diff(job_comparison$loglik), 1), big.mark = ",")` and AIC falls
by `r format(round(-diff(job_comparison$AIC), 1), big.mark = ",")`. A boundary
likelihood-ratio statistic of `r round(job_lr$LR, 1)` provides overwhelming
evidence against (q=0). Substantively, allowing legitimate current-job resets
reduces the estimated gross tenure-contamination probability from
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * job_comparison$tenure_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * job_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`%. It therefore
explains an important subset of tenure discontinuities, but most tenure
inconsistency is still assigned to the broader contamination mechanism. The
weighted entry and exit rates move only modestly, so the extension improves the
measurement model without overturning the employment-flow results.

## Matching-panel robustness

Panel A remains the preferred and main dataset. Panels B and C change only the
record-matching restrictions and diagnose whether the reset mechanism is
disproportionately supported by weaker links.

```{r matching-model-comparison}
match_show <- matching_comparison[, c("panel", "observations",
  "job_change_prob", "posterior_job_change_rate",
  "status_misclassification", "tenure_contamination",
  "timegap_contamination", "weighted_entry", "weighted_exit")]
names(match_show) <- c("Panel", "N", "Job reset", "Posterior reset",
  "Status error", "Tenure error", "Timegap error", "Entry", "Exit")
match_show$Panel <- paste("Panel", match_show$Panel)
match_show$N <- format(match_show$N, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE)
match_show[, 3:9] <- lapply(match_show[, 3:9], function(x)
  sprintf("%.3f", x))
knitr::kable(match_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Job-change model under alternative matching restrictions")
```

The reset probability is nearly unchanged between Panels A and B
(`r sprintf('%.2f', 100 * matching_comparison$job_change_prob[1])`% versus
`r sprintf('%.2f', 100 * matching_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`%) and declines
to `r sprintf('%.2f', 100 * matching_comparison$job_change_prob[3])`% in Panel
C. By contrast, status misclassification falls from
`r sprintf('%.2f', 100 * matching_comparison$status_misclassification[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.2f', 100 * matching_comparison$status_misclassification[3])`%,
and tenure contamination falls from
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * matching_comparison$tenure_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * matching_comparison$tenure_contamination[3])`%.
Stricter matching therefore removes substantial measurement inconsistency but
does not eliminate the current-job reset signal. The modest decline under C
also cautions against interpreting every reset as a genuine job-to-job move.

# 5. Numerical validation and recovery

## Optimizer stability

The high-reset dispersed start converges to the established optimum, and a
tighter refinement changes the reset estimate only from
`r sprintf('%.4f', 100 * validation_starts$job_change_prob[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.4f', 100 * validation_interval$estimate)`%. A deliberately low
start converges to an inferior local mode, with a log likelihood lower by
`r format(round(validation_starts$loglik[1]-validation_starts$loglik[2], 1), big.mark=',')`.
Multiple starts and likelihood-based selection are therefore required.

Reoptimizing all 14 nuisance parameters at seven fixed reset probabilities
gives a provisional 95% profile-likelihood interval of
[`r sprintf('%.3f', 100 * validation_interval$lower)`%,
`r sprintf('%.3f', 100 * validation_interval$upper)`%]. The local quadratic
fit has (R^2=`r sprintf('%.5f', validation_interval$quadratic_R2)`). This
interval describes the implemented likelihood; it is not yet suitable for the
paper because the recovery check below fails.

## Full-likelihood recovery

Three samples of 20,000 observations were simulated from the intended model
and re-estimated from both low and high reset starts. The reset and tenure-error
parameters are not recovered without systematic bias.

```{r recovery-table}
recover_show <- validation_recovery[, c("parameter", "truth",
  "mean_estimate", "bias")]
recover_show$parameter <- c("Job reset", "Status error", "Tenure error",
  "Timegap error")
names(recover_show) <- c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean estimate", "Bias")
recover_show[, 2:4] <- lapply(recover_show[, 2:4], function(x)
  sprintf("%.3f", x))
knitr::kable(recover_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Full-likelihood recovery diagnostic")
```

In particular, a true reset probability of
`r sprintf('%.3f', 100 * validation_recovery$truth[1])`% is estimated at
`r sprintf('%.3f', 100 * validation_recovery$mean_estimate[1])`% on average,
while tenure contamination rises from
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * validation_recovery$truth[3])`% to
`r sprintf('%.1f', 100 * validation_recovery$mean_estimate[3])`%. This is not
just small-sample variation: with 100,000 simulated observations, the numerical
likelihood scores at the generating values remain strongly nonzero
(`r round(validation_score$q_score, 1)` for resets and
`r round(validation_score$eps_score, 1)` for tenure contamination).

The leading cause is a units problem in the continuous-density approximation.
Mixture branches contain different numbers of independent tenure-density
evaluations, and hence have different physical units, but the current
likelihood adds them directly. Clean clock restrictions also create singular
components that are mixed with ordinary continuous densities. Since tenure is
constructed from a reported start **month**, the defensible repair is to model
tenure in discrete months: replace marginal densities by monthly interval
probabilities and replace the continuous within-quarter reset density by a
probability over possible start months. The job-change result should not be
promoted to Table 7 until that repair restores simulation recovery.

## Discrete-month repair and re-estimation

The repaired likelihood treats a reported tenure of (m) months as the mass

\[
P(m/12 \leq D < (m+1)/12),
\]

rather than evaluating a continuous density at (m/12). Clean tenure clocks
advance by exactly three months between quarterly interviews. A latent spell
that begins between waves, or a current-job reset within a persistent
employment spell, starts at 0, 1, or 2 reported months. This puts every branch
of the mixture on the same probability scale. The ingestion also retains
2,753 genuine zero-month reports and drops two records that previously received
an artificial quarter-month floor because no valid tenure report was available.

```{r monthly-comparison}
monthly_show <- monthly_comparison[, c("model", "loglik", "AIC",
  "job_change_prob", "status_misclassification", "tenure_contamination",
  "timegap_contamination", "entry_rate", "exit_rate")]
names(monthly_show) <- c("Model", "Log likelihood", "AIC", "Job reset",
  "Status error", "Tenure error", "Timegap error", "Entry", "Exit")
monthly_show[, 4:9] <- lapply(monthly_show[, 4:9], function(x)
  sprintf("%.3f", x))
monthly_show[, 2:3] <- lapply(monthly_show[, 2:3], function(x)
  format(round(x, 1), big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE))
knitr::kable(monthly_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Panel A discrete-month tenure likelihood")
```

The preferred reset fit estimates a quarterly current-job reset probability of
`r sprintf('%.3f', 100*monthly_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`%, almost exactly
equal to its posterior mean of
`r sprintf('%.3f', 100*monthly_comparison$posterior_job_change_rate[2])`%.
Allowing resets raises the log likelihood by
`r format(round(diff(monthly_comparison$loglik), 1), big.mark=',')` and gives a
boundary LR statistic of `r round(monthly_lr$LR, 1)`. Relative to the no-reset
monthly model, it lowers tenure contamination only modestly, from
`r sprintf('%.2f', 100*monthly_comparison$tenure_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.2f', 100*monthly_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`%.

All three reset starts converge near the same solution: their reset estimates
range from `r sprintf('%.3f',100*min(monthly_starts$job_change_prob))`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*max(monthly_starts$job_change_prob))`%, and their log
likelihoods differ by less than
`r sprintf('%.1f',diff(range(monthly_starts$loglik)))`.

Six additional full-likelihood recovery fits use three independent samples at
each of 10,000 and 40,000 observations. All converge, and high dispersed starts
at both sample sizes do not improve the likelihood.

```{r monthly-recovery-grid}
keep <- monthly_recovery_grid$parameter %in%
  c("job_change_prob", "pi", "eps", "eps_d")
rec_show <- monthly_recovery_grid[keep,
  c("n", "parameter", "truth", "mean", "bias", "rmse")]
rec_show$parameter <- c("Job reset", "Status error", "Tenure error",
  "Timegap error")[match(rec_show$parameter,
    c("job_change_prob", "pi", "eps", "eps_d"))]
names(rec_show) <- c("N", "Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "Bias", "RMSE")
rec_show$N <- format(rec_show$N, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE)
rec_show[, 3:6] <- lapply(100*rec_show[, 3:6], function(x)
  sprintf("%.3f", x))
rownames(rec_show) <- NULL
knitr::kable(rec_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Repeated full-likelihood recovery (percentage points)")
```

At 40,000 observations, mean bias is only
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*monthly_recovery_grid$bias[monthly_recovery_grid$n==40000 & monthly_recovery_grid$parameter=='job_change_prob'])`
percentage points for resets,
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*monthly_recovery_grid$bias[monthly_recovery_grid$n==40000 & monthly_recovery_grid$parameter=='pi'])`
for status error,
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*monthly_recovery_grid$bias[monthly_recovery_grid$n==40000 & monthly_recovery_grid$parameter=='eps'])`
for tenure contamination, and
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*monthly_recovery_grid$bias[monthly_recovery_grid$n==40000 & monthly_recovery_grid$parameter=='eps_d'])`
for timegap contamination. RMSE also falls with sample size. The likelihood
scores at the generating parameters change sign across replications rather
than showing the systematic direction found under the continuous model. These
checks support accepting the discrete likelihood repair. A larger simulation
would still be required to assess confidence-interval coverage directly.

## Analytical and profile inference

The full 15-parameter numerical observed-information matrix is positive
definite and full rank. Its minimum eigenvalue is
`r sprintf('%.4g',monthly_hessian$minimum_eigenvalue)`, and its condition number
is `r sprintf('%.1f',monthly_hessian$condition_number)`. Delta-method standard
errors therefore propagate the joint uncertainty in all transition hazards,
contamination probabilities, initial employment, and job resets.

```{r monthly-inference}
order_q <- c("entry_rate", "exit_rate", "status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination", "timegap_contamination", "initial_employment",
  "job_change_prob")
inf_show <- monthly_inference[match(order_q, monthly_inference$quantity),
  c("quantity", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]
inf_show$quantity <- c("Entry", "Exit", "Status error", "Tenure error",
  "Timegap error", "Initial employment", "Job reset")
names(inf_show) <- c("Quantity", "Estimate", "SE", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%")
inf_show[,2:5] <- lapply(100*inf_show[,2:5], function(x) sprintf("%.3f",x))
knitr::kable(inf_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Discrete-month model: analytical standard errors (percent)")
```

The reset estimate is
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_profile_interval$estimate)`% with analytical SE
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_profile_interval$analytical_se)` percentage
points. Reoptimizing all 14 nuisance parameters at each fixed reset probability
gives a 95% profile interval of
[`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_profile_interval$lower)`%,
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_profile_interval$upper)`%]. It is nearly
identical to the Wald interval, and the profile quadratic has
(R^2=`r sprintf('%.5f',monthly_profile_interval$quadratic_R2)`). Thus profile
asymmetry is negligible around the interior optimum.

The discrete model materially changes the substantive allocation. Compared
with the continuous reset fit, the reset probability falls from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*job_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`% to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*monthly_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`%, status
misclassification rises from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*job_comparison$status_misclassification[2])`% to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*monthly_comparison$status_misclassification[2])`%, and
tenure contamination falls from
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*job_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`% to
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*monthly_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`%. Entry also
falls, while exit changes less. Log likelihoods across the continuous and
monthly models are not comparable because one uses densities and the other
uses discrete probability masses.

\newpage

## Matching-panel sensitivity of the corrected model

The identical corrected monthly specification was re-estimated on Panels B and
C. Panel A remains the main sample; the stricter panels are sensitivity checks,
not alternative preferred datasets.

```{r monthly-matching-comparison}
mm_show <- monthly_matching[, c("panel", "observations", "job_change_prob",
  "posterior_job_change_rate", "status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination", "timegap_contamination", "entry_rate", "exit_rate")]
names(mm_show) <- c("Panel", "N", "Job reset", "Posterior reset",
  "Status error", "Tenure error", "Timegap error", "Entry", "Exit")
mm_show$N <- format(mm_show$N, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE)
mm_show[,3:9] <- lapply(100*mm_show[,3:9], function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x))
knitr::kable(mm_show, booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Corrected discrete-month model under alternative matching restrictions (percent)")
```

The reset estimate declines monotonically from
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_matching$job_change_prob[1])`% in Panel A to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_matching$job_change_prob[2])`% in B and
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*monthly_matching$job_change_prob[3])`% in C. Status
misclassification falls from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*monthly_matching$status_misclassification[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*monthly_matching$status_misclassification[3])`%, tenure
contamination from
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*monthly_matching$tenure_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*monthly_matching$tenure_contamination[3])`%, and timegap
contamination from
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*monthly_matching$timegap_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*monthly_matching$timegap_contamination[3])`%. Entry is
nearly unchanged in B and modestly lower in C; exit also falls slightly. Thus
stricter matching removes some apparent transition and duration inconsistency,
but it does not eliminate the estimated current-job reset process.

All six B/C optimizations converged normally. Within each panel, low, main, and
high reset starts reach log likelihoods agreeing within
`r sprintf('%.2f', max(tapply(monthly_matching_starts$loglik,
  monthly_matching_starts$panel, function(x) diff(range(x)))[c('B','C')]))`
log-likelihood units; reset estimates span only
`r sprintf('%.4f',100*max(tapply(monthly_matching_starts$job_change_prob,
  monthly_matching_starts$panel, function(x) diff(range(x)))[c('B','C')]))`
percentage points within either Panel B or C.

\newpage

## Reporting-process extensions

The five nested Panel A versions can be compared coefficient by coefficient.
The first rules out job resets and persistent gross reports. The second adds a
job-reset probability but treats gross start-date reports as independent over
time. The third estimates whether a gross report retains the preceding
reported start-date anchor. The fourth instead allows gross reports to follow
the empirically prominent January-heaping pattern. The fifth adds a correlated
whole-year revision of the previously reported start date.

```{r nested-model-coefficients}
no_reset <- monthly_fits$no_reset$params
independent <- monthly_fits$reset$params
persistent <- persistent_fits$persistent$params
heaping <- heaping_fits$heaping$params
revision <- revision_fits$revision$params

duration_labels <- c("0-3 months", "3-12 months", "1-3 years",
                     "3-5 years", "5+ years")
coefficient_labels <- c(
  "Initial employment probability",
  "Status misclassification probability",
  "Tenure contamination probability",
  "Timegap contamination probability",
  paste0("Exit hazard: ", duration_labels),
  paste0("Entry hazard: ", duration_labels),
  "Job-reset probability",
  "Gross-report persistence probability",
  "January-heaping probability",
  "Whole-year revision probability"
)

extract_coefficients <- function(x, persistence = 0, heaping = 0,
                                 revision = 0) {
  c(x$alpha, x$pi, x$eps, x$eps_d, x$lambda_g, x$lambda_d,
    x$job_change_prob, persistence, heaping, revision)
}
fmt_coefficient <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)

coef_table <- data.frame(
  Coefficient = coefficient_labels,
  `No reset` = fmt_coefficient(extract_coefficients(no_reset)),
  `Independent gross` = fmt_coefficient(extract_coefficients(independent)),
  `Persistent gross` = fmt_coefficient(extract_coefficients(
    persistent, persistent$tenure_report_persistence)),
  `January heap` = fmt_coefficient(extract_coefficients(
    heaping, heaping=heaping$tenure_heaping_prob)),
  `January + year revision` = fmt_coefficient(extract_coefficients(
    revision, heaping=revision$tenure_heaping_prob,
    revision=revision$tenure_year_revision_prob)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
reset_row <- match("Job-reset probability",coef_table$Coefficient)
persistence_row <- match("Gross-report persistence probability",
  coef_table$Coefficient)
heaping_row <- match("January-heaping probability",coef_table$Coefficient)
revision_row <- match("Whole-year revision probability",
  coef_table$Coefficient)
coef_table[reset_row, "No reset"] <- "0 (fixed)"
coef_table[persistence_row,
  c("No reset", "Independent gross", "January heap",
    "January + year revision")] <-
  "0 (fixed)"
coef_table[persistence_row, "Persistent gross"] <- "0 (boundary)"
coef_table[heaping_row,
  c("No reset", "Independent gross", "Persistent gross")] <- "0 (fixed)"
coef_table[revision_row,
  c("No reset", "Independent gross", "Persistent gross",
    "January heap")] <- "0 (fixed)"

fit_rows <- data.frame(
  Coefficient = c("Log likelihood", "AIC", "Number of parameters"),
  `No reset` = c(
    format(round(monthly_fits$no_reset$loglik, 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    format(round(monthly_fits$comparison$AIC[1], 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    monthly_fits$comparison$parameters[1]
  ),
  `Independent gross` = c(
    format(round(monthly_fits$reset$loglik, 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    format(round(monthly_fits$comparison$AIC[2], 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    monthly_fits$comparison$parameters[2]
  ),
  `Persistent gross` = c(
    format(round(persistent_fits$persistent$loglik, 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    format(round(persistent_fits$comparison$AIC[2], 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    persistent_fits$comparison$parameters[2]
  ),
  `January heap` = c(
    format(round(heaping_fits$heaping$loglik, 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    format(round(heaping_fits$comparison$AIC[2], 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    heaping_fits$comparison$parameters[2]
  ),
  `January + year revision` = c(
    format(round(revision_fits$revision$loglik, 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    format(round(revision_fits$comparison$AIC[2], 1), big.mark = ",",
           scientific = FALSE),
    revision_fits$comparison$parameters[2]
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(rbind(coef_table, fit_rows), booktabs = TRUE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste("Natural-scale coefficients across nested corrected",
                  "discrete-month models (Panel A)"))
```

All probability and hazard coefficients are shown on the natural zero-to-one
scale. Exit and entry hazards are annualized piecewise-constant hazards for the
indicated duration band. The job-reset coefficient is the probability within
an observed quarterly interval; gross-report persistence is the conditional
probability that a contaminated report retains the previous reported anchor.
January heaping is the conditional probability that a gross report is drawn
from the marginal duration law restricted to an implied January start date.
Whole-year revision is the conditional probability that an eligible new gross
report preserves the previous reported start month but changes its year.
“Fixed” denotes a nesting restriction, while “boundary” denotes an estimated
coefficient whose constrained MLE is zero.

### Persistent reported-start-date extension

The first reporting-process extension allows a consecutive gross tenure report
within the same latent job to retain the preceding reported start-date anchor
with probability (rho). Otherwise it draws a new marginal anchor. Clean tenure
reports remain exactly consistent with the true employment spell, job changes
start a new segment, and the timegap process is unchanged. The independent
gross-report model is nested exactly at (rho=0).

```{r persistent-reporting-comparison}
rate_names <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "tenure_report_persistence")
pr_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","Persistence","Log likelihood","AIC"),
  Independent=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(persistent_comparison[1,rate_names])),
    format(round(persistent_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(persistent_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  Persistent=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(persistent_comparison[2,rate_names])),
    format(round(persistent_comparison$loglik[2],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(persistent_comparison$AIC[2],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(pr_show)[2:3] <- c("Independent gross reports","Persistent gross anchor")
knitr::kable(pr_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Persistent reported-start-date extension (rates in percent)")
```

The constrained MLE is exactly at (rho=0). Consequently, every other reported
rate is unchanged, the likelihood-ratio statistic is
`r sprintf('%.1f',persistent_lr$LR)`, and adding the unused parameter raises
AIC by two. The converged middle start reaches the numerical lower bound
(`r sprintf('%.6f',100*persistent_starts$tenure_report_persistence[2])`%),
while the high start returns to the same basin from (rho=0.90) but reaches the
iteration cap only after matching its likelihood closely. A low start finds an
inferior local solution approximately
`r format(round(max(persistent_starts$loglik)-persistent_starts$loglik[1],1),big.mark=',')`
log-likelihood units below the boundary solution. The exact nested fit is
therefore retained rather than a slightly inferior numerical approximation to
zero.

This boundary result is not caused by an intrinsically unidentified
persistence parameter. In a 12,000-record simulation with true (rho=0.60), the
conditional likelihood peaks at
`r sprintf('%.3f',persistent_profile$rho[which.max(persistent_profile$loglik)])`
on the reported grid, and the two full-likelihood starts converge to
`r paste(sprintf('%.3f',persistent_recovery_fits$tenure_report_persistence),collapse=' and ')`.
The likelihood can therefore distinguish substantial persistence, although
the best estimate is downward biased by
`r sprintf('%.3f',-persistent_recovery$bias[persistent_recovery$parameter=='tenure_report_persistence'])`
in this single moderate-size simulation. More replications would be needed for
coverage or bias correction.

Substantively, the data do not support this particular one-parameter mechanism
in addition to the clean-clock and independent gross-report branches. This is
not evidence that respondents never repeat start dates: clock-consistent
sequences are already assigned to the clean branch, and a persistently wrong
anchor can be observationally similar for jobs that began before the panel.
The next reporting extension should therefore focus on structured start-month
heaping or a persistent offset tied to jobs whose start is bounded by an
observed entry or reset, rather than adding further unrestricted persistence.

\newpage

### January-heaped gross-report extension

The next extension uses the strongest calendar pattern in the audit. For an
interview in nominal month (M), a tenure report of (m) months implies a January
start when $m \bmod 12=M-1$. Conditional on a gross tenure report, the model
now uses

\[
f^{gross}(m\mid M)=(1-h)f(m)+h
\frac{\mathbf{1}\{m\bmod 12=M-1\}f(m)}
{P_f(m\bmod 12=M-1)}.
\]

Thus the heaped component preserves the estimated marginal duration shape but
conditions it on an implied January start. It is normalized exactly, adds one
parameter, and nests the independent-gross model at (h=0). Nominal interview
months are retained when the likelihood cells are collapsed.

```{r calendar-heaping-comparison}
heap_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","prior_heaped_tenure_report_prob")
heap_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
    "Gross-and-heaped tenure report","Log likelihood","AIC"),
  Independent=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    heaping_comparison[1,heap_rates])),
    format(round(heaping_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(heaping_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  January_heaping=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    heaping_comparison[2,heap_rates])),
    format(round(heaping_comparison$loglik[2],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(heaping_comparison$AIC[2],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(heap_show)[2:3] <- c("Independent gross","January-heaped gross")
knitr::kable(heap_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="January-heaped gross-report extension (rates in percent)")
```

All three starts converge normally. They estimate (h) between
`r sprintf('%.5f',min(heaping_starts$gross_january_heaping_prob))` and
`r sprintf('%.5f',max(heaping_starts$gross_january_heaping_prob))`, while their
log likelihoods differ by only
`r sprintf('%.3f',diff(range(heaping_starts$loglik)))`. The preferred estimate
is `r sprintf('%.2f',100*heaping_comparison$gross_january_heaping_prob[2])`%:
conditional on a gross tenure report, roughly one quarter of reports are
assigned to the January-conditioned component. Because gross reporting itself
has probability `r sprintf('%.2f',100*heaping_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`%,
their prior product is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*heaping_comparison$prior_heaped_tenure_report_prob[2])`%
of otherwise correctly classified employed-wave tenure reports.

Fit improves sharply: the log likelihood rises by
`r format(round(diff(heaping_comparison$loglik),1),big.mark=',')`, AIC falls by
`r format(round(-diff(heaping_comparison$AIC),1),big.mark=',')`, and the
boundary likelihood-ratio statistic is
`r format(round(heaping_lr$LR,1),big.mark=',')`. Entry changes from
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$entry_rate[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$entry_rate[2])`%, exit from
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$exit_rate[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$exit_rate[2])`%, and the job-reset
probability from `r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$job_change_prob[1])`%
to `r sprintf('%.3f',100*heaping_comparison$job_change_prob[2])`%. The main
transition conclusions are therefore stable, while the reporting likelihood
fits the calendar pattern much better.

The observed survey-weighted January share averages
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*heaping_observed$observed_january_share[2])`% across the
three waves. This is not directly comparable to (h): clean reports and the
ordinary marginal gross distribution can also imply January starts. Nor does
the model establish that January reports are errors; genuine seasonal hiring
or a coding convention could generate the same concentration. The parameter
should be described as a structured reporting component unless external
validation separates those mechanisms.

```{r calendar-heaping-recovery}
heap_recovery_show <- heaping_recovery
heap_recovery_show$parameter <- c("January heaping","Job reset",
  "Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error")
for (nm in c("truth","estimate","bias"))
  heap_recovery_show[[nm]] <- sprintf("%.4f",heap_recovery_show[[nm]])
names(heap_recovery_show) <- c("Parameter","Truth","Estimate","Bias")
knitr::kable(heap_recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Calendar-heaping recovery check (6,000 simulated records)")
```

In the recovery exercise, the truth is (h=0.40). The conditional optimum is
0.385, and two dispersed joint starts converge to estimates agreeing within
`r sprintf('%.5f',diff(range(heaping_recovery_fits$tenure_heaping_prob)))`.
The small downward error in (h) does not materially distort the reset, status,
or timegap-error probabilities. This supports identification of the added
component, although repeated simulations would be required for bias and
coverage statements.

```{r calendar-heaping-inference}
heap_se_names <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob")
heap_se_labels <- c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error",
  "Timegap error","Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross")
heap_se_show <- heaping_inference[match(heap_se_names,
  heaping_inference$quantity),c("estimate","se","lower","upper")]
heap_se_show <- 100*heap_se_show
heap_se_show <- data.frame(Quantity=heap_se_labels,
  Estimate=sprintf("%.3f",heap_se_show$estimate),
  `Analytical SE`=sprintf("%.3f",heap_se_show$se),
  `95% lower`=sprintf("%.3f",heap_se_show$lower),
  `95% upper`=sprintf("%.3f",heap_se_show$upper),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(heap_se_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Observed-information and delta-method inference for January heaping (percent)")
```

The full 16-parameter observed-information matrix is positive definite and
full rank. Its condition number is 97.2, providing no numerical indication of
a locally unidentified heaping parameter. These are analytical
observed-information standard errors, not bootstrap standard errors.

### Correlated whole-year date revisions

The next nested component targets the second prominent calendar pattern. Let
$m_{t-1}$ be the previous gross tenure report, let $c=m_{t-1}+3\Delta$ be its
exact continuation after $\Delta$ panel intervals, and let $S_{t-1}$ be its
implied reported start month. A whole-year revision draws the current report
from the marginal duration law conditional on preserving $S_{t-1}$ while
excluding (c):

\[
 f^{year}(m_t\mid S_{t-1},c)=
 \frac{\mathbf{1}\{S(m_t)=S_{t-1},\ m_t\ne c\}f(m_t)}
 {P_f\{S(m)=S_{t-1}\}-f(c)}.
\]

For eligible consecutive gross reports within the same latent job, the model
uses the ordinary January-heaping gross law with probability $1-\omega$ and
this different-year law with probability $\omega$. It is normalized exactly
and nests the preceding model at $\omega=0$. This is distinct from the failed
persistence extension: persistence repeats the exact reported date, whereas
this component changes the year but preserves the month.

```{r calendar-revision-comparison}
revision_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","whole_year_revision_prob")
revision_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
    "Whole-year revision, conditional on eligible gross pair",
    "Log likelihood","AIC"),
  January_heaping=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    revision_comparison[1,revision_rates])),
    format(round(revision_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(revision_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  Whole_year_revision=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    revision_comparison[2,revision_rates])),
    format(round(revision_comparison$loglik[2],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(revision_comparison$AIC[2],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(revision_show)[2:3] <- c("January heaping",
  "January + whole-year revisions")
knitr::kable(revision_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Correlated whole-year date-revision extension (rates in percent)")
```

The preferred high start converges normally at
$\omega=`r sprintf('%.4f',revision_comparison$whole_year_revision_prob[2])`$.
The central start reaches
`r sprintf('%.4f',revision_starts$whole_year_revision_prob[revision_starts$start=='main'])`
but is
`r sprintf('%.1f',max(revision_starts$loglik)-revision_starts$loglik[revision_starts$start=='main'])`
log-likelihood points lower. The deliberately low 0.03 start stops in an
inferior local mode at its initial revision probability, more than
`r format(round(max(revision_starts$loglik)-min(revision_starts$loglik),1),big.mark=',')`
points below the preferred solution. It is therefore a numerical warning, not
a competing substantive estimate: multistart likelihood selection is needed.
Relative to January heaping alone, the preferred log likelihood changes by
`r format(round(diff(revision_comparison$loglik),1),big.mark=',')`, AIC changes
by `r format(round(diff(revision_comparison$AIC),1),big.mark=',')`, and the
boundary LR statistic is `r format(round(revision_lr$LR,1),big.mark=',')`.
Entry moves from `r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$entry_rate[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$entry_rate[2])`%, exit from
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$exit_rate[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$exit_rate[2])`%, and tenure
contamination from
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$tenure_contamination[1])`% to
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_comparison$tenure_contamination[2])`%.

The raw survey-weighted share of employed-report pairs whose implied start
month is unchanged but whose year differs ranges from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*min(revision_observed$observed_whole_year_revision_share))`%
to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*max(revision_observed$observed_whole_year_revision_share))`%.
This is not directly $\omega$: the observed share mixes clean clocks, job
changes, gross reports, and status error, whereas $\omega$ is conditional on
an eligible latent gross-report pair.

```{r calendar-revision-recovery}
revision_recovery_show <- revision_recovery
revision_recovery_show$parameter <- c("Whole-year revision","January heaping",
  "Job reset","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error")
for (nm in c("truth","estimate","bias"))
  revision_recovery_show[[nm]] <- sprintf("%.4f",revision_recovery_show[[nm]])
names(revision_recovery_show) <- c("Parameter","Truth","Estimate","Bias")
knitr::kable(revision_recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Whole-year revision recovery check (6,000 simulated records)")
```

With a generating value of $\omega=0.45$, the conditional likelihood optimum
is 0.456. Two dispersed joint starts recover 0.443 and 0.458. The best fit also
recovers January heaping within 0.0005 and tenure contamination within 0.0040
of their generating values, supporting separate identification of the two
calendar components in this diagnostic sample.

```{r calendar-revision-inference}
revision_se_names <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","whole_year_revision_prob")
revision_se_labels <- c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error",
  "Timegap error","Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
  "Whole-year revision, conditional on eligible gross pair")
revision_se_show <- revision_inference[match(revision_se_names,
  revision_inference$quantity),c("estimate","se","lower","upper")]
revision_se_show <- 100*revision_se_show
revision_se_show <- data.frame(Quantity=revision_se_labels,
  Estimate=sprintf("%.3f",revision_se_show$estimate),
  `Analytical SE`=sprintf("%.3f",revision_se_show$se),
  `95% lower`=sprintf("%.3f",revision_se_show$lower),
  `95% upper`=sprintf("%.3f",revision_se_show$upper),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(revision_se_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Observed-information and delta-method inference for the whole-year revision model (percent)")
```

The full 17-parameter observed-information matrix is positive definite and
full rank. Its condition number is
`r sprintf('%.1f',revision_hessian$condition_number)`. The analytical standard
error of $\omega$ is
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*revision_inference$se[revision_inference$quantity=='whole_year_revision_prob'])`
percentage points. The nuisance-adjusted profile interval is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*revision_profile_interval$profile_lower)`--
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*revision_profile_interval$profile_upper)`%, compared with
the analytical interval
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*revision_profile_interval$analytical_lower)`--
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*revision_profile_interval$analytical_upper)`%. Thus the
preferred local solution has regular local curvature; this does not by itself
establish that the reporting process is correctly specified.

### Parametric predictive checks and source of fit improvement

The fitted-parameter checks below compare observed Panel A moments with 40
simulated samples of 50,000 records. They assess replication of the observed
calendar patterns conditional on the fitted parameters; they do not integrate
over parameter uncertainty.

```{r calendar-revision-predictive}
predictive_metrics <- c("all_employed_reports_january_start",
  "consecutive_pairs_exact","consecutive_pairs_whole_year",
  "consecutive_pairs_other")
predictive_labels <- c("January start month, all employed reports",
  "Exact continuation, consecutive employed pairs",
  "Whole-year revision, consecutive employed pairs",
  "Other revision, consecutive employed pairs")
pred <- revision_predictive[revision_predictive$metric %in% predictive_metrics,]
pred$Measure <- predictive_labels[match(pred$metric,predictive_metrics)]
pred$Model <- ifelse(pred$model=="January heaping","January only",
  "January + year revision")
pred_show <- reshape(pred[,c("Measure","Model","predicted_mean")],
  idvar="Measure",timevar="Model",direction="wide")
names(pred_show) <- sub("predicted_mean\\.","",names(pred_show))
pred_show$Observed <- pred$observed[match(pred_show$Measure,pred$Measure)]
pred_show <- pred_show[match(predictive_labels,pred_show$Measure),]
pred_show <- pred_show[,c("Measure","January only",
  "January + year revision","Observed")]
for (nm in names(pred_show)[-1]) pred_show[[nm]] <-
  sprintf("%.2f",100*pred_show[[nm]])
knitr::kable(pred_show,booktabs=TRUE,row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Fitted-parameter predictive checks for observed calendar patterns (percent)")
```

The revision component moves the predicted whole-year-revision share in the
intended direction, from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*pred$predicted_mean[pred$Model=='January only' & pred$metric=='consecutive_pairs_whole_year'])`%
to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*pred$predicted_mean[pred$Model=='January + year revision' & pred$metric=='consecutive_pairs_whole_year'])`%,
but the observed share is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*pred$observed[pred$metric=='consecutive_pairs_whole_year'][1])`%.
None of the four observed moments lies within the corresponding 95% simulation
envelope. In particular, predicted January starts remain near 13.6% compared
with 26.4% observed. A conditional January probability of about 24% among
gross reports cannot reproduce the aggregate month distribution when only
about 22% of tenure reports use that gross component. Genuine hiring
seasonality, calendar-specific clean reports, or both may therefore be
missing from the baseline start-month law.

```{r calendar-revision-decomposition}
decomp_show <- revision_decomposition
decomp_show$pattern <- c(
  "Exact continuation"="Exact continuation",
  "At least one exact continuation"="Exact continuation",
  "At least one whole-year revision"="At least one whole-year revision",
  "Fewer than two employed reports"="Fewer than two employed reports",
  "Other multiple employed reports"="Other multiple-employed pattern"
)[decomp_show$pattern]
decomp_show <- data.frame(Pattern=unname(decomp_show$pattern),
  `Population share (%)`=sprintf("%.2f",100*decomp_show$population_share),
  `Log-likelihood gain`=sprintf("%.1f",decomp_show$loglik_gain),
  `Share of net gain (%)`=sprintf("%.1f",100*decomp_show$gain_share),
  check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(decomp_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Decomposition of the whole-year extension's log-likelihood gain")
```

All of the positive fit improvement comes from the 6.16% of weighted records
with at least one observed whole-year date revision. Their gain exceeds the
net gain because the extension loses about 3,083 log-likelihood points on
other patterns. This concentration is substantively informative, but the
offsetting deterioration and failed predictive checks show that the current
correlated branch is too narrow. It requires both adjacent reports to be
gross. The following extension implements the first repair; start-month
seasonality remains a separate next step.

\clearpage

### Revisions of preceding clean reports

Let $\eta$ denote the probability that a gross current tenure report draws
from the same normalized whole-year revision law when its preceding observed
tenure report was clean. The existing gross-to-gross probability $\omega$
remains separate. Thus $\eta=0$ reproduces the preceding 17-parameter model
exactly, while the 18-parameter extension distinguishes which type of report
supplies the preceding date anchor. Missing tenure reports do not erase an
anchor within the same latent job, but a latent job change does.

```{r clean-anchor-revision-comparison}
clean_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","gross_anchor_revision_prob",
  "clean_anchor_revision_prob")
clean_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
    "Gross-anchor whole-year revision",
    "Clean-anchor whole-year revision","Log likelihood","AIC"),
  Nested=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    clean_revision_comparison[1,clean_rates])),
    format(round(clean_revision_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(clean_revision_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  Extended=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    clean_revision_comparison[2,clean_rates])),
    format(round(clean_revision_comparison$loglik[2],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(clean_revision_comparison$AIC[2],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(clean_show)[2:3] <- c("Gross-anchor revisions only",
  "Gross + clean-anchor revisions")
knitr::kable(clean_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Clean-anchor whole-year revision extension (rates in percent)")
```

The extension improves the log likelihood by
`r format(round(diff(clean_revision_comparison$loglik),1),big.mark=',')`
points and lowers AIC by
`r format(round(-diff(clean_revision_comparison$AIC),1),big.mark=',')`.
The boundary LR statistic is
`r format(round(clean_revision_lr$LR,1),big.mark=',')`.
Starts at 3%, 25%, and 65% all converge near
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*clean_revision_comparison$clean_anchor_revision_prob[2])`%
for $\eta$. Allowing clean anchors reduces $\omega$ from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*clean_revision_comparison$gross_anchor_revision_prob[1])`%
to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*clean_revision_comparison$gross_anchor_revision_prob[2])`%,
while entry, exit, status error, and the two marginal contamination rates move
by less than 0.04 percentage points. The new channel therefore reallocates
the reporting process without materially changing the employment-transition
interpretation.

\clearpage

```{r clean-anchor-revision-inference}
clean_se_names <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","whole_year_revision_prob",
  "clean_anchor_revision_prob")
clean_se_labels <- c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error",
  "Timegap error","Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
  "Gross-anchor whole-year revision","Clean-anchor whole-year revision")
clean_se_show <- clean_revision_inference[match(clean_se_names,
  clean_revision_inference$quantity),c("estimate","se","lower","upper")]
clean_se_show <- 100*clean_se_show
clean_se_show <- data.frame(Quantity=clean_se_labels,
  Estimate=sprintf("%.3f",clean_se_show$estimate),
  `Analytical SE`=sprintf("%.3f",clean_se_show$se),
  `95% lower`=sprintf("%.3f",clean_se_show$lower),
  `95% upper`=sprintf("%.3f",clean_se_show$upper),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(clean_se_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Observed-information inference for the clean-anchor extension (percent)")
```

The 18-parameter observed-information matrix is positive definite and full
rank, with condition number
`r sprintf('%.1f',clean_revision_hessian$condition_number)`. The analytical
standard error of $\eta$ is
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*clean_revision_inference$se[clean_revision_inference$quantity=='clean_anchor_revision_prob'])`
percentage points. The delta-method correlation between $\eta$ and $\omega$
is
`r sprintf('%.3f',cov2cor(clean_revision_inference_full$vcov_quantities)['clean_anchor_revision_prob','whole_year_revision_prob'])`.
The channels are related but the local information does not indicate a nearly
singular reallocation.

```{r clean-anchor-revision-recovery}
clean_recovery_show <- clean_revision_recovery
clean_recovery_show$parameter <- c("Clean-anchor revision",
  "Gross-anchor revision","January heaping","Tenure error","Job reset",
  "Status error")
for (nm in c("truth","estimate","bias"))
  clean_recovery_show[[nm]] <- sprintf("%.4f",clean_recovery_show[[nm]])
names(clean_recovery_show) <- c("Parameter","Truth","Estimate","Bias")
knitr::kable(clean_recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Clean-anchor revision recovery check (8,000 simulated records)")
```

Both recovery starts converge to the same likelihood and estimate $\eta$ at
about 0.325 when its generating value is 0.35. The corresponding estimate of
$\omega$ is about 0.244 rather than 0.204. This demonstrates joint
recoverability, while the offsetting finite-sample biases caution against
interpreting the two probabilities too finely without a larger repeated
recovery design.

```{r clean-anchor-revision-predictive}
clean_pred_metrics <- c("all_employed_reports_january_start",
  "consecutive_pairs_exact","consecutive_pairs_whole_year",
  "consecutive_pairs_other")
clean_pred_labels <- c("January start month, all employed reports",
  "Exact continuation, consecutive employed pairs",
  "Whole-year revision, consecutive employed pairs",
  "Other revision, consecutive employed pairs")
cp <- clean_revision_predictive[
  clean_revision_predictive$metric %in% clean_pred_metrics,]
cp$Measure <- clean_pred_labels[match(cp$metric,clean_pred_metrics)]
cp$Model <- ifelse(cp$model=="Gross-anchor revisions only",
  "Gross-anchor only","Gross + clean-anchor")
cp_show <- reshape(cp[,c("Measure","Model","predicted_mean")],
  idvar="Measure",timevar="Model",direction="wide")
names(cp_show) <- sub("predicted_mean\\.","",names(cp_show))
cp_show$Observed <- cp$observed[match(cp_show$Measure,cp$Measure)]
cp_show <- cp_show[match(clean_pred_labels,cp_show$Measure),
  c("Measure","Gross-anchor only","Gross + clean-anchor","Observed")]
for (nm in names(cp_show)[-1]) cp_show[[nm]] <-
  sprintf("%.2f",100*cp_show[[nm]])
knitr::kable(cp_show,booktabs=TRUE,row.names=FALSE,
  caption="Predictive checks after allowing clean-anchor revisions (percent)")
```

The targeted whole-year-revision prediction rises from 4.10% to 5.79%, closer
to the observed 7.01%, while other revisions fall from 35.58% to about 33.8%
against 28.29% observed. The checks nevertheless still fail: exact
continuations remain too low and January starts remain near 13.4% rather than
26.4%. The extension explains an important part of the date-revision pattern,
but it does not repair the missing baseline calendar distribution.

```{r clean-anchor-revision-decomposition}
clean_decomp_show <- data.frame(
  Pattern=clean_revision_decomposition$pattern,
  `Population share (%)`=sprintf("%.2f",
    100*clean_revision_decomposition$population_share),
  `Log-likelihood gain`=sprintf("%.1f",
    clean_revision_decomposition$loglik_gain),
  `Share of net gain (%)`=sprintf("%.1f",
    100*clean_revision_decomposition$gain_share),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(clean_decomp_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Likelihood gain from allowing clean-anchor revisions")
```

As intended, the positive gain is concentrated among the 6.16% of weighted
records with a whole-year revision. Their gain is partly offset by lower fit
for exact continuations and other multiple-employed patterns. The next model
should therefore estimate a genuine start-month distribution shared by clean
and gross reports before adding further dependence or AR(2) dynamics.

\clearpage

### Flexible baseline start-month distribution

The next extension replaces the implicit uniform distribution of job-start
months with 12 probabilities, estimated through 11 logits relative to
December. The duration mass is multiplied by the probability of its implied
calendar start month and renormalized separately for each interview month.
The same distribution enters clean and gross marginal tenure reports and the
0--2 month support for latent entries and job resets. Uniform probabilities
reproduce the preceding 18-parameter likelihood exactly. The gross-only
January-heaping branch and the two whole-year revision probabilities remain
separate.

```{r start-month-baseline-comparison}
start_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","gross_anchor_revision_prob",
  "clean_anchor_revision_prob")
start_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","January heaping, conditional on gross",
    "Gross-anchor whole-year revision",
    "Clean-anchor whole-year revision","Log likelihood","AIC"),
  Uniform=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    start_month_comparison[1,start_rates])),
    format(round(start_month_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(start_month_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  Flexible=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    start_month_comparison[2,start_rates])),
    format(round(start_month_comparison$loglik[2],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(start_month_comparison$AIC[2],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(start_show)[2:3] <- c("Uniform baseline","Flexible baseline")
knitr::kable(start_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Shared flexible baseline start-month distribution (rates in percent)")
```

The flexible distribution improves the log likelihood by
`r format(round(diff(start_month_comparison$loglik),1),big.mark=',')` points
and lowers AIC by
`r format(round(-diff(start_month_comparison$AIC),1),big.mark=',')` despite 11
additional parameters. The LR statistic for equal month probabilities is
`r format(round(start_month_lr$LR,1),big.mark=',')` on 11 degrees of freedom.
Entry, exit, status error, and tenure and timegap contamination each move by
less than 0.2 percentage points. The transition interpretation is therefore
stable. In contrast, the gross-specific January-heaping probability falls
from
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*start_month_comparison$gross_january_heaping_prob[1])`%
to approximately zero. January concentration belongs in the shared baseline
calendar distribution rather than in an error process used only by gross
reports.

\clearpage

```{r start-month-baseline-distribution}
month_show <- data.frame(Month=start_month_distribution$month,
  `Observed reports`=sprintf("%.2f",
    100*start_month_distribution$observed_report_share),
  `Estimated baseline`=sprintf("%.2f",
    100*start_month_distribution$estimated_baseline),
  Uniform=sprintf("%.2f",100*start_month_distribution$uniform),
  check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(month_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Observed and estimated job-start month distributions (percent)")
```

The estimated baseline puts
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*start_month_distribution$estimated_baseline[1])`% of
start dates in January, followed by March, February, and April. December has
only
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*start_month_distribution$estimated_baseline[12])`%.
This strongly non-uniform pattern explains why the earlier gross-only heaping
component could not reproduce the aggregate data: most January concentration
is common to clean and gross reports.

```{r start-month-baseline-predictive}
pred_metrics <- c("consecutive_pairs_exact","consecutive_pairs_whole_year",
  "consecutive_pairs_other","start_month_1")
pred_labels <- c("Exact continuation","Whole-year revision","Other revision",
  "January start month")
sp <- start_month_predictive[start_month_predictive$model=="Flexible baseline" &
  start_month_predictive$metric %in% pred_metrics,]
sp <- sp[match(pred_metrics,sp$metric),]
pred_show <- data.frame(Measure=pred_labels,
  Predicted=sprintf("%.2f",100*sp$predicted_mean),
  Observed=sprintf("%.2f",100*sp$observed),
  `Within 95% simulation envelope`=ifelse(sp$within_95,"Yes","No"),
  check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(pred_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Predictive checks for the flexible baseline (percent)")
```

The month distribution is repaired: 11 of 12 observed month shares lie inside
their fitted-parameter simulation envelopes. Whole-year revisions rise to
6.89%, close to 7.01% observed. However, exact continuations remain too low
(60.7% versus 64.7%) and other revisions too high (32.5% versus 28.3%). The
remaining misspecification is therefore serial dependence in reporting, not
baseline calendar seasonality.

\clearpage

```{r start-month-baseline-recovery}
best_recovery <- start_month_recovery_fits[
  which.max(start_month_recovery_fits$loglik),]
recovery_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("January probability","Month-distribution RMSE",
    "Gross-anchor revision","Clean-anchor revision","Tenure error",
    "Status error"),
  Truth=c(start_month_recovery$truth[1],NA,0.065764500,0.104707950,
    0.218171810,0.030195474),
  Estimate=c(start_month_recovery$estimate[1],best_recovery$month_rmse,
    best_recovery$gross_anchor_revision_prob,
    best_recovery$clean_anchor_revision_prob,
    best_recovery$tenure_contamination,
    best_recovery$status_misclassification))
recovery_show$Truth <- ifelse(is.na(recovery_show$Truth),"--",
  sprintf("%.4f",recovery_show$Truth))
recovery_show$Estimate <- sprintf("%.4f",recovery_show$Estimate)
knitr::kable(recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Joint recovery check (2,000 simulated records)")
```

Uniform and reversed conditional starts converge to essentially the same
likelihood, and the safeguarded joint optimizer converges before a capped
central refinement. The 12-month distribution is recovered with RMSE about
0.0044. The two revision channels show more small-sample reallocation, so
their sum and predictive implications remain more reliable than a fine
comparison of their separate probabilities. Full observed-information
inference for all 29 parameters remains to be completed; the near-zero
gross-only January-heaping estimate is a boundary quantity and should not be
given a regular Wald interpretation.

\clearpage

### Exact reported-start-date retention

The next nested extension lets a gross current tenure report retain the
preceding reported job-start date exactly, regardless of whether the preceding
report was clean or gross. Let $\rho$ denote this retention probability. If
the anchor is not retained, the report follows the existing whole-year
revision versus marginal-redraw mixture. Thus $\rho=0$ reproduces the flexible
baseline likelihood exactly and the two revision parameters retain their
conditional interpretation.

```{r exact-anchor-comparison}
anchor_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_anchor_revision_prob","clean_anchor_revision_prob",
  "exact_anchor_retention_prob")
anchor_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","Gross-anchor whole-year revision",
    "Clean-anchor whole-year revision","Exact-anchor retention",
    "Log likelihood","AIC"),
  Baseline=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    exact_anchor_comparison[1,anchor_rates])),
    format(round(exact_anchor_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(exact_anchor_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  Retention=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    exact_anchor_comparison[3,anchor_rates])),
    format(round(exact_anchor_comparison$loglik[3],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(exact_anchor_comparison$AIC[3],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
names(anchor_show)[2:3] <- c("Flexible baseline","Exact retention")
knitr::kable(anchor_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Exact reported-start-date retention (rates in percent)")
```

The polished joint estimate is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*exact_anchor_comparison$exact_anchor_retention_prob[3])`%.
The log likelihood rises by
`r format(round(exact_anchor_comparison$loglik[3]-
  exact_anchor_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=',')` points; the corresponding
one-parameter LR statistic is
`r format(round(exact_anchor_lr$LR,1),big.mark=',')`. Entry and exit rates move
only from 2.28% and 4.14% to 2.31% and 4.14%. The substantive transition result
is therefore stable. Tenure contamination rises from 21.82% to
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*exact_anchor_comparison$tenure_contamination[3])`% because
the enlarged gross-report process can now include both retained and redrawn
dates.

```{r exact-anchor-refinement}
refine_keep <- exact_anchor_refinement$stage %in%
  c("continued","low","high","promoted","polished")
refine_show <- exact_anchor_refinement[refine_keep,
  c("stage","loglik","gain_over_incumbent","exact_anchor_retention")]
refine_show$gain_over_incumbent <- refine_show$loglik-
  exact_anchor_refinement$loglik[exact_anchor_refinement$stage=="continued"]
refine_show$stage <- c("First central block","Low-retention start",
  "High-retention start","Continued joint fit","Conditional polish")
refine_show$loglik <- format(round(refine_show$loglik,1),big.mark=",",
  scientific=FALSE)
refine_show$gain_over_incumbent <- sprintf("%+.2f",
  refine_show$gain_over_incumbent)
refine_show$exact_anchor_retention <- sprintf("%.2f",
  100*refine_show$exact_anchor_retention)
names(refine_show) <- c("Fit","Log likelihood","Gain","Retention (%)")
rownames(refine_show) <- NULL
knitr::kable(refine_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Longer refinement of the exact-retention model")
```

The continued joint refinement raises the log likelihood by
`r sprintf('%.2f',exact_anchor_refinement$loglik[
  exact_anchor_refinement$stage=='polished']-
  exact_anchor_refinement$loglik[exact_anchor_refinement$stage=='continued'])`
points relative to the first central block. Low- and high-retention screens
are hundreds of likelihood points worse. The final scalar
polish adds 0.001 point, so the point estimates are practically stable even
though the capped joint blocks retain optimizer convergence code 1. Full
observed-information inference for the 30 parameters remains outstanding.

```{r exact-anchor-predictive}
anchor_metrics <- c("exact_continuation","whole_year_revision",
  "other_revision")
anchor_labels <- c("Exact continuation","Whole-year revision",
  "Other revision")
ap <- exact_anchor_predictive[
  exact_anchor_predictive$metric %in% anchor_metrics,]
ap <- ap[order(match(ap$metric,anchor_metrics),ap$model),]
ap_show <- data.frame(Measure=rep(anchor_labels,each=2),
  Model=ap$model,Predicted=sprintf("%.2f",100*ap$predicted_mean),
  Observed=sprintf("%.2f",100*ap$observed),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(ap_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Predictive implications of exact-anchor retention (percent)")
```

Exact continuations rise from
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*ap$predicted_mean[ap$model=='Flexible baseline' & ap$metric=='exact_continuation'])`%
to
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*ap$predicted_mean[ap$model=='Exact-anchor retention' & ap$metric=='exact_continuation'])`%,
toward the observed 64.7%, and other revisions fall from
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*ap$predicted_mean[ap$model=='Flexible baseline' & ap$metric=='other_revision'])`%
to
`r sprintf('%.1f',100*ap$predicted_mean[ap$model=='Exact-anchor retention' & ap$metric=='other_revision'])`%,
toward 28.3%. Whole-year revisions
remain essentially exact at 7.0%. The extension therefore targets the intended
serial feature but does not close the full gap. Likelihood gains are concentrated
in records containing a mixture of continuation patterns and are offset by
losses among single-pattern records. A richer local date-revision kernel remains
warranted.

```{r exact-anchor-recovery}
anchor_recovery_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Generating retention","Mean recovered retention",
    "Recovery RMSE","Minimum estimate","Maximum estimate",
    "Mean LR against zero"),
  Value=c(exact_anchor_recovery$truth,
    exact_anchor_recovery$mean_estimate,exact_anchor_recovery$rmse,
    exact_anchor_recovery$minimum,exact_anchor_recovery$maximum,
    exact_anchor_recovery$mean_LR_zero))
anchor_recovery_show$Value <- sprintf("%.4f",anchor_recovery_show$Value)
knitr::kable(anchor_recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Conditional recovery of exact-anchor retention (20 samples of 5,000)")
```

Holding nuisance parameters at their generating values, the new probability
is recovered with small mean bias and an RMSE of about three percentage points.
All 20 replications produce a positive interior estimate and strongly favor
retention over the nested zero value. This establishes conditional
identification, but is intentionally an easier check than joint recovery.

```{r exact-anchor-joint-recovery}
joint_selected <- exact_anchor_joint_fits[exact_anchor_joint_fits$selected,]
transition_recovery <- data.frame(
  Sample=paste("Replication",joint_selected$replication),
  `True entry`=100*joint_selected$true_entry_rate,
  `Estimated entry`=100*joint_selected$entry_rate,
  `True exit`=100*joint_selected$true_exit_rate,
  `Estimated exit`=100*joint_selected$exit_rate,
  check.names=FALSE)
for (j in 2:ncol(transition_recovery))
  transition_recovery[[j]] <- sprintf("%.3f",transition_recovery[[j]])
knitr::kable(transition_recovery,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Full 30-parameter recovery: transition rates (percent)")

joint_parameters <- c("exact_anchor_retention","eps","pi",
  "clean_anchor_revision","gross_anchor_revision")
joint_labels <- c("Exact-anchor retention","Tenure contamination",
  "Status misclassification","Clean-anchor revision",
  "Gross-anchor revision")
jr <- exact_anchor_joint_recovery[
  match(joint_parameters,exact_anchor_joint_recovery$parameter),]
joint_recovery_show <- data.frame(Parameter=joint_labels,
  Truth=sprintf("%.2f",100*jr$truth),
  Mean=sprintf("%.2f",100*jr$mean_estimate),
  Bias=sprintf("%+.2f",100*jr$mean_bias),
  RMSE=sprintf("%.2f",100*jr$rmse),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(joint_recovery_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Full 30-parameter recovery: reporting probabilities (percentage points)")
```

All three simulated samples can be re-estimated from near and dispersed starts.
The selected pooled entry- and exit-rate RMSEs are
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*sqrt(mean(joint_selected$entry_rate_bias^2)))` and
`r sprintf('%.3f',100*sqrt(mean(joint_selected$exit_rate_bias^2)))` percentage
points. The third replication is less favorable than the first two, with
entry and exit errors of
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*joint_selected$entry_rate_bias[3])` and
`r sprintf('%+.3f',100*joint_selected$exit_rate_bias[3])` points, respectively.
The aggregate transition result is nevertheless much more robust than
individual duration-hazard bins. By
contrast, the reporting decomposition is weakly separated at this sample size:
the retention RMSE is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*jr$rmse[jr$parameter=='exact_anchor_retention'])` points,
and clean- and gross-anchor revision probabilities partly offset one another.
The exercise shows that the full likelihood is estimable, but three
replications do not establish
precise finite-sample identification of every reporting component.

```{r exact-anchor-opg-inference}
opg_names <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_january_heaping_prob","gross_anchor_revision_prob",
  "clean_anchor_revision_prob","exact_anchor_retention_prob")
opg_labels <- c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error",
  "Timegap error","Job reset","Gross-only January heaping",
  "Gross-anchor revision","Clean-anchor revision","Exact-anchor retention")
oi <- exact_anchor_opg[match(opg_names,exact_anchor_opg$quantity),]
opg_show <- data.frame(Quantity=opg_labels,
  Estimate=sprintf("%.3f",100*oi$estimate),
  `Analytical SE`=sprintf("%.3f",100*oi$se),
  `95% interval`=sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]",100*oi$lower,100*oi$upper),
  check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(opg_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="OPG analytical inference for the exact-retention model (percent)")
```

The 30-parameter score matrix is full rank, but its condition number is
`r format(signif(exact_anchor_opg_diagnostics$condition_number,3),scientific=TRUE)`,
consistent with weak local separation. The exact-retention standard error is
0.574 percentage points under this analytical approximation. The most
important natural-scale correlations are 0.885 between exact retention and
overall tenure contamination, and -0.540 between the clean- and gross-anchor
revision probabilities. These correlations agree with the simulation evidence
that reporting channels can offset one another. Gross-only January heaping is
effectively on the boundary: its regular interval crosses zero by a wide
margin, so its Wald standard error should be treated only as a diagnostic.
The OPG calculation uses 61 likelihood evaluations. A resumable central
observed-Hessian calculation has also been implemented; its first 48 of 1,801
points are cached, but the exact calculation is not yet complete.

\clearpage

### Local reported-start-date revisions

The next nested extension addresses near-anchor changes directly. Conditional
on a gross current tenure report, the preceding reported start date is first
retained exactly with probability $\rho$. If it is not retained, the report
receives a non-zero local revision with probability $\kappa$; otherwise it
passes to the existing whole-year-revision versus marginal-redraw mixture. The
local revision is a normalized discrete-Laplace kernel over one to six months
in either direction, with fixed three-month scale and truncation at zero
tenure. Consequently, $\kappa=0$ reproduces the exact-anchor model exactly and
zero-month changes are not counted twice.

```{r local-anchor-comparison}
local_rates <- c("entry_rate","exit_rate","status_misclassification",
  "tenure_contamination","timegap_contamination","job_change_prob",
  "gross_anchor_revision_prob","clean_anchor_revision_prob",
  "exact_anchor_retention_prob","local_anchor_revision_prob")
local_show <- data.frame(
  Quantity=c("Entry","Exit","Status error","Tenure error","Timegap error",
    "Job reset","Gross-anchor whole-year revision",
    "Clean-anchor whole-year revision","Exact-anchor retention",
    "Local revision conditional on no exact retention","Log likelihood",
    "AIC"),
  `Exact retention`=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    local_anchor_comparison[1,local_rates])),
    format(round(local_anchor_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(local_anchor_comparison$AIC[1],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),
  `Local revision`=c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(
    local_anchor_comparison[3,local_rates])),
    format(round(local_anchor_comparison$loglik[3],1),big.mark=",",
      scientific=FALSE),format(round(local_anchor_comparison$AIC[3],1),
      big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE)),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(local_show,booktabs=TRUE,
  caption="Local reported-start-date revision extension (rates in percent)")
```

The conditional local-revision estimate is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*local_anchor_comparison$local_anchor_revision_prob[3])`%.
Because exact retention is tried first, its corresponding unconditional share
among eligible gross reports is
`r sprintf('%.2f',100*(1-local_anchor_comparison$exact_anchor_retention_prob[3])*
  local_anchor_comparison$local_anchor_revision_prob[3])`%. The log likelihood
increases by
`r format(round(local_anchor_comparison$loglik[3]-
  local_anchor_comparison$loglik[1],1),big.mark=',')` points, giving a boundary
