# 9. Four-wave AR(1) bridge to the AR(2) extension

The next substantive extension is employment-history dependence, rather than
further refinement of the separation between duration-reliability classes.
The four-wave bridge retains the preferred three-wave measurement model:
discrete-month tenure, piecewise duration hazards, current-job resets,
calendar and local reporting revisions, joint timegap contamination, and
equal prior weights for the two reliability classes. No additional employment
heterogeneity class has been introduced.

`EM-tenure/R/four_wave_eps.R` sums over all 16 four-wave latent employment
histories. `EM-tenure/estimate_monthly_four_wave_ar1.R` prepares Panel A,
caches incremental optimisation blocks, and constructs a waves 1--3
comparison using exactly the people and weights in the four-wave sample.
The initial employment probability remains free. The likelihood is estimated
directly, not with the old three-wave EM sufficient-statistic updates.

## Sample and estimates

**Subsequent validation warning:** Section 10 identifies a timegap likelihood
normalization defect, repaired in Section 11. The estimates below remain
saved, numerically converged pre-repair results. Section 12 reports the
separate empirical refit under the repaired likelihood when validated.

There are 317,437 records with four observed employment statuses and 316,889
with the required state-appropriate duration reports (548 exclusions).
The likelihood collapses these to 101,916 distinct observation cells without
changing their weighted contribution. Zero-month tenure is retained;
unreported-state durations remain missing. Never-worked reports follow the
same recoding convention as in the three-wave model. Interview months remain
nominal quarter-end months, not recovered exact interview dates.

```{r four-wave-bridge-results, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
bridge_dir <- file.path("..", "EM-tenure", "output", "results",
  "job_change_monthly", "four_wave_ar1")
if (!dir.exists(bridge_dir)) bridge_dir <- file.path("EM-tenure", "output",
  "results", "job_change_monthly", "four_wave_ar1")
bridge_path <- file.path(bridge_dir, "stage_summary_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(file.path(bridge_dir, "convergence_summary_latest.csv")))
  bridge_path <- file.path(bridge_dir, "convergence_summary_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(bridge_path)) {
  bridge <- read.csv(bridge_path)
  selected <- if ("independently_converged" %in% names(bridge))
    seq_len(nrow(bridge)) else unique(c(1L, which.max(bridge$loglik)))
  bridge_fields <- c("entry_rate", "exit_rate", "status_misclassification",
    "initial_employment", "loglik")
  bridge_table <- data.frame(Measure = c("Entry rate", "Exit rate",
    "Misclassification rate", "Initial employment", "Log likelihood"))
  bridge_titles <- c(preliminary="Preliminary", exact1="Refined",
    start_minus="Start (-)", start_plus="Start (+)", start="Inherited")
  for (j in selected) {
    title <- if (bridge$stage[j] %in% names(bridge_titles))
      unname(bridge_titles[bridge$stage[j]]) else bridge$stage[j]
    values <- as.numeric(unlist(bridge[j, bridge_fields], use.names=FALSE))
    bridge_table[[title]] <- c(sprintf("%.5f", values[1:4]),
      formatC(values[5], format="f", digits=2, big.mark=","))
  }
  print(knitr::kable(bridge_table, digits=5,
    caption="Four-wave AR(1): numerical refinement and starting-point checks"))
} else cat("Four-wave optimisation checkpoints are not yet consolidated.\n")
```

The preliminary column is an unconverged checkpoint. All three completed
refinement runs have optimizer code zero and final maximum projected central
scores between $1.5\times10^{-6}$ and $3.0\times10^{-6}$ per observation,
below the declared $10^{-5}$ criterion.
The optimizer's scaled tolerance is chosen to imply this unscaled criterion;
the latter is checked separately after termination. Start (+) has the highest
log likelihood and is selected in `converged_comparison_latest.rds`. The
three likelihoods differ by at most 0.056; entry, exit, and status-error
rates differ by less than 0.00004 percentage points. This supports numerical
stability of these rates, not precise identification of every reporting
parameter.

Entry and exit rates pool the three quarterly intervals, weighting each
individual-interval by the survey weight and posterior probability of the
relevant origin state. Misclassification is the common employment-status
error probability, not a duration-contamination probability. The reliability
mixture's tenure and timegap midpoint parameters should not be interpreted
as mean contamination probabilities.

Relative to the preliminary four-wave point, quarterly entry rises from
2.446% to 2.603%, exit rises slightly from 4.033% to 4.060%, status
misclassification falls from 2.822% to 2.765%, and initial employment is
essentially unchanged (48.685% versus 48.705%). The log likelihood improves
by about 665.8. This is a numerical improvement within the **same model and
sample**, not a test of a new specification. The preliminary fit understated
entry more than exit; the broad finding of substantial misclassification
remains. Likelihood levels on different three-wave and four-wave samples
must not be compared as an LR test. The optional same-person three-wave
re-estimation is omitted at the author's request.

## Checks and outstanding work

The continuation now has a separately validated compiled evaluator
(`four_wave_fast.R` and `src/four_wave_monthly.cpp`). It uses the reference R
probability tables and caches repeated spell and reporting-pattern calculations;
no likelihood terms or model restrictions are changed. On the saved full sample,
the log-likelihood difference is less than $10^{-7}$ and maximum posterior
differences are below $10^{-13}$. Perturbed-parameter, zero-status-error,
disabled-revision, and serial/parallel comparisons also pass. A benchmark using
eight threads takes about 1.3 seconds per full likelihood evaluation, rather
than roughly a minute for the earlier R implementation.

`refine_four_wave_ar1_fast.R` jointly refines all 33 parameters, retains
improving checkpoints, and checks a central-difference projected score after
the optimizer stops. The diagonal of the saved three-wave information matrix
is used only for numerical parameter scaling; it is not a substitute for
four-wave standard errors and requires no three-wave re-estimation.
The same-person three-wave re-estimation has been dropped from the work plan
at the author's request.

For the final continuation, category-averaged and missing-duration risks are
calculated with exact piecewise-exponential integrals. The integral splits at
the duration-hazard knots and their quarter-shifted counterparts. Fifty tests
against independent numerical integration and limiting cases pass. At the
saved preliminary point this changes the total log likelihood by about
$-0.000037$ and the largest posterior probability by less than $2\times10^{-8}$;
its purpose is to remove amplified quadrature noise from the numerical score,
not to change the model. The three-wave estimator is not modified. Central
finite differences are used for the final joint refinement.

- Tests pass for all 16 histories, posterior normalization, the zero-status-error
  limit, three-wave joint-timegap equivalence, and four-wave timegap probability
  normalization. Preparation tests cover zero tenure, never-worked recoding,
  missing flags, and exclusion of invalid state-appropriate durations.
- Sharing and compressing repeated job-segment calculations reproduces the
  saved full-sample likelihood and posterior probabilities exactly. This is
  a computational change, not a model change.
- Accepted bounded optimisation steps are flagged as non-converged. Early
  checkpoints with a zero code are corrected when consolidated; step
  acceptance is not evidence that the likelihood has been maximized.
- All three four-wave runs pass optimizer and central-score convergence
  checks. The full-sample likelihood and posterior agree with the R reference
  at the fitted parameters. Starting-point checks are saved separately in
  `multistart_summary_latest.csv`; all fit objects and diagnostics are retained.
- The two nearby starts perturb all 33 transformed parameters by
  $+0.05\sin(j)$ and $-0.05\sin(j)$, respectively, from the saved
  `start_multistart_exact.rds` point. Continuations resume saved checkpoints
  without applying the perturbation again.
- Nearby-start agreement is a numerical stability check, not proof of a global
  optimum or strong identification of the reliability-class separation.
- The first four-wave simulation gate fails (Section 10); Section 11 records
  the repair and renewed validation. Analytical standard errors and the
  duration-model AR(2) extension have not been estimated.

# 10. Four-wave simulation-recovery gate

## Changes and scope

- Extended the existing sequential simulator to four waves, retaining its
  three-wave defaults and adding the exact piecewise-risk option.
- Generated three independent samples of 20,000 records at the selected
  Panel A four-wave parameters (seeds 260904--260906). These are simulations,
  not additional empirical panels or bootstrap replications.
- Checked the mean record-level score at the known truth before fitting.
  Its Monte Carlo standard error is the sample standard deviation of the
  score divided by the square root of the simulated sample size.
- Added exhaustive probability-mass and timegap-clock checks. No empirical
  fit or likelihood formula was changed, and no simulation recovery fit was
  run after these gates failed.

## Results

The short-duration entry-hazard score is negative in all three samples
(individual standardized scores -5.18, -5.26, and -5.50). The pooled mean is
-0.01225 with Monte Carlo standard error 0.001331: a standardized discrepancy
of -9.20. This fails the conservative screening threshold of five Monte Carlo
standard errors. It establishes a generator/likelihood mismatch, not a
precisely quantified bias in the empirical entry rate.

```{r four-wave-recovery-score, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
recovery_dir <- file.path("..", "EM-tenure", "output", "results",
  "job_change_monthly", "four_wave_ar1", "recovery")
if (!dir.exists(recovery_dir)) recovery_dir <- sub("^../", "", recovery_dir)
score_file <- file.path(recovery_dir, "sequential_score_summary_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(score_file)) {
  score <- read.csv(score_file)
  fields <- c("log_hd1", "log_hd3", "pi", "alpha")
  score <- score[match(fields, score$parameter), ]
  shown <- data.frame(Parameter=c("Entry log-hazard: 0--3 months",
    "Entry log-hazard: 1--3 years", "Status-error logit",
    "Initial-employment logit"),
    `Mean score`=score$mean_score, `Monte Carlo SE`=score$mcse,
    `Standardized score`=score$z_score, check.names=FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(shown, digits=c(0,6,6,2),
    caption="Generator/likelihood score check: 60,000 simulated records"))
}
```

An independent finite-support check exposes a defect in the likelihood itself.
The illustrative nested case uses constant tenure hazards of 20 per year,
uniform start months, no job resets or serial tenure-revision channels,
initial employment 0.5, tenure contamination 0.2, and timegap hazards
either constant at 0.4 or equal to (4, 1, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2). It enumerates all
four-wave observed status/duration combinations with tenure 0--24 months,
including all seven timegap categories: 1,048,576 cells.

```{r four-wave-recovery-mass, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
mass_file <- file.path(recovery_dir, "probability_mass_m24.csv")
if (file.exists(mass_file)) {
  mass <- read.csv(mass_file)[c(7,6,4,8), ]
  shown <- data.frame(`Duration-dependent entry`=ifelse(mass$varying_hazard,"Yes","No"),
    `Status error`=mass$status_error,
    `Timegap error`=ifelse(mass$timegap_error<1e-7,"Approximately zero","0.30"),
    `Total probability`=sprintf("%.9f",mass$probability_mass),check.names=FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(shown,caption="Exhaustive normalization check in a nested example"))
}
```

When duration dependence, status errors, and timegap contamination are all
present, total mass is **0.999327180679**, rather than one. Increasing the
tenure cutoff from 12 to 24 months leaves the discrepancy essentially
unchanged. A conservative omitted-tail bound at 24 months is below
$1.7\times10^{-10}$; it cannot explain the missing mass of about 0.000673.
The R reference and compiled implementation give the same result at the
12-month cutoff. Constant-hazard and near-zero-error controls sum to one
within numerical/tail tolerance. This is a counterexample to normalization,
not an estimate of the defect's size at the empirical parameters.

## Diagnosis and interpretation

- **Future-report-dependent fallback:** the four-wave E-step uses a joint
  timegap likelihood only when an entire latent nonemployment spell is
  observed as nonemployment. Otherwise it falls back to adjacent-pair terms.
  Thus a fourth reported employment status can change the likelihood factor
  for the first three timegap reports. In the illustrative case, the joint
  three-report distribution and pairwise fallback differ by 0.2286 in total
  variation. Individually normalized components do not guarantee a normalized
  full likelihood when transition risks also depend on the reports.
- **A separate simulator mismatch:** the simulator retains a continuous
  nonemployment clock and ages it across waves. The likelihood instead
  multiplies category-to-category transition probabilities, effectively
  discarding within-category information from earlier reports. Exact
  interval-intersection probabilities and that category-Markov approximation
  differ even with negligible timegap contamination (total variation 0.02143
  in the same illustrative hazard case).
- These findings are about probability construction, not merely weak
  identification of the two reliability classes. They do not establish how
  much the empirical entry, exit, or misclassification rates will change.
  Earlier numerical convergence and implementation-equivalence checks still
  hold, but the four-wave results are not yet validated for interpretation.
  Earlier normalization checks covered individual emissions and posterior
  weights, not the sum of the complete joint probability over observable
  records; those are different tests.

The repair should use one joint timegap-spell likelihood for every observed
subset, integrating missing or contaminated reports and retaining the clean
clock's interval restrictions across all waves. The simulator must implement
that same probability law. Re-run normalization and score checks first; only
then run the small parameter-recovery fits. This repair was deferred at the
initial validation stage and subsequently authorized; see Section 11.

Reproduction scripts are `validate_four_wave_simulation.R`,
`audit_four_wave_probability_mass.R`, and `summarise_four_wave_recovery.R`.
For the mass audit, use `FOUR_WAVE_MASS_MAX_MONTH=24` for the tight-tail check;
use 12 with `FOUR_WAVE_MASS_REFERENCE=true` for the independent R comparison.
Set `FOUR_WAVE_TIMEGAP_CLOCK=legacy_pairwise` to reproduce these historical
failures. The consolidated `recovery/recovery_status_latest.rds` records the
failed gates, zero recovery fits, and unchanged empirical estimates.

# 11. Repaired continuous timegap clock and recovery

## Changes

- Replaced the four-wave joint/pairwise fallback with one joint timegap
  likelihood for every latent nonemployment spell and every observed subset.
- Each clean report restricts the same spell-start duration. Missing reports
  are integrated out, and all contamination patterns are summed. Information
  from earlier categories is retained rather than discarded at each wave.
- Applied the same calculation in the R reference and compiled evaluator.
  The existing sequential simulator already retains and ages this clock;
  its four-wave exact-risk option now matches the repaired likelihood.
- Kept the initial timegap distribution, transition-risk formulas, tenure
  reporting model, and three-wave estimator unchanged. In particular, this
  repair does not introduce a new within-quarter distribution for timegap at
  a nonemployment spell's onset. That remains a separate modelling question.
- Preserved legacy evaluation explicitly as `legacy_pairwise`; repaired
  four-wave evaluation defaults to `continuous_joint`. Historical fit objects
  and failed diagnostics are not overwritten.

For a clean report in category interval $[a_t,b_t)$ at offset $t$, the
spell-start clock satisfies $D_0\in[a_t-t\Delta,b_t-t\Delta)$. Its joint
clean-report probability is

$$
P\left\{\max(0,\max_t(a_t-t\Delta))\le D_0
<\min_t(b_t-t\Delta)\right\},\qquad \Delta=0.25.
$$

An empty intersection has probability zero. Gross reports instead contribute
their marginal category probabilities; unobserved reports impose no
restriction. Mixture weights retain the existing clock-specific reliability
classes. This enforces clean-clock consistency across all observed waves
without requiring every status report to be correct.

## Probability and score checks

All eight exhaustive probability cases now sum to one within numerical
tolerance, including the former failing case. Summing out any report gives
the same joint distribution for the remaining reports. Fifty-six new unit
checks cover observed subsets, boundary contamination probabilities, interval
intersections, and missing early reports. The repaired full-sample compiled
likelihood agrees with R within $4.6\times10^{-8}$; maximum posterior
differences are below $1.3\times10^{-14}$.

Repeating the same three 20,000-person simulation samples removes the score
failure: the short-duration entry-hazard discrepancy falls from -9.20 to
+1.86 Monte Carlo standard errors. No pooled score among the 33 parameters
exceeds 1.87 in absolute value. These checks support the repaired probability
law; they do not by themselves establish finite-sample recovery or precision.

```{r four-wave-clock-repair-checks, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
repaired_dir <- file.path(dirname(recovery_dir),"recovery_continuous_clock")
new_score_file <- file.path(repaired_dir,"sequential_score_summary_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(new_score_file)) {
  old <- read.csv(file.path(recovery_dir,"sequential_score_summary_latest.csv"))
  new <- read.csv(new_score_file)
  keep <- c("log_hd1","log_hd3","pi","alpha")
  comparison <- data.frame(Parameter=c("Entry log-hazard: 0--3 months",
    "Entry log-hazard: 1--3 years","Status-error logit","Initial-employment logit"),
    Legacy=old$z_score[match(keep,old$parameter)],
    Repaired=new$z_score[match(keep,new$parameter)])
  print(knitr::kable(comparison,digits=2,
    caption="Standardized score at the generating parameters: before and after repair"))
}
```

## Small full-parameter recovery exercise

`estimate_four_wave_recovery.R` estimates all 33 parameters on two independent
5,000-person samples, using two nearby starting points for the first sample
and one for the second (seeds 261004 and 261005). It uses the same bounded
likelihood optimization and a separate projected central-score tolerance of
$10^{-5}$. The saved empirical scaling vector is only a numerical
preconditioner. No nuisance parameter is fixed at its generating value.

```{r four-wave-clock-recovery-fits, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
fits_file <- file.path(repaired_dir,"fit_summary_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(fits_file)) {
  recovery_fits <- read.csv(fits_file)
  for (rep in unique(recovery_fits$replication)) {
    fits <- recovery_fits[recovery_fits$replication==rep,]
    tab <- data.frame(Measure=c("Entry rate","Exit rate","Misclassification rate",
      "Initial employment"),
      Generating=c(fits$entry_truth[1],fits$exit_truth[1],
        fits$pi_truth[1],fits$alpha_truth[1]))
    for (j in seq_len(nrow(fits))) tab[[fits$start[j]]] <-
      c(fits$entry_estimate[j],fits$exit_estimate[j],fits$pi_estimate[j],fits$alpha_estimate[j])
    print(knitr::kable(tab,digits=5,caption=paste("Simulation recovery: sample",rep)))
  }
  print(knitr::kable(recovery_fits[c("replication","start","n","converged","score","loglik")],
    digits=c(0,0,0,0,8,3),caption="Recovery convergence diagnostics"))
} else cat("Full-parameter recovery fits are not yet consolidated.\n")
```

The generating transition rates use the true parameters and their posterior
risk weights on the same simulated sample, so differences isolate parameter
estimation rather than differences in sample composition. Full hazard
coefficients are saved in `coefficient_recovery_latest.csv` and shown below;
fit objects also
retain all reporting parameters and numerical diagnostics. This is a small
implementation/recovery check, not a large Monte Carlo bias study or a
bootstrap standard-error exercise. Empirical Panel A rates are not updated
by these simulated fits.

All three fits converge with maximum projected central scores between
$2.54\times10^{-6}$ and $2.93\times10^{-6}$. The two starts for sample 1 differ
by less than 0.001 log-likelihood units and 0.00013 percentage points in the
main rates. Across the two samples, entry, exit, and status misclassification
are each within 0.16 percentage points of their generating values. Initial
employment differs by -1.10 and +0.16 percentage points, respectively.
The high short-duration entry hazard and lower long-duration hazards remain
visible in the recovered coefficients. These results support the repaired
implementation and approximate recovery of economically relevant quantities;
two samples do not establish finite-sample unbiasedness, precise reliability
separation, or a globally unique optimum.

```{r four-wave-clock-recovery-hazards, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
coef_file <- file.path(repaired_dir,"coefficient_recovery_latest.csv")
if (file.exists(coef_file) && file.exists(fits_file)) {
  coef <- read.csv(coef_file)
  fits <- read.csv(fits_file)
  keep <- c(paste0("entry_hazard_",1:5),paste0("exit_hazard_",1:5))
  bands <- c("0--3 months","3--12 months","1--3 years","3--5 years","5+ years")
  tab <- data.frame(Hazard=c(paste("Entry:",bands),paste("Exit:",bands)),
    Generating=coef$truth[match(keep,coef$parameter)])
  for (rep in unique(fits$replication)) {
    candidates <- fits[fits$replication==rep & fits$converged,]
    if (!nrow(candidates)) next
    label <- candidates$start[which.max(candidates$loglik)]
    selected <- coef[coef$replication==rep & coef$start==label,]
    tab[[paste("Sample",rep)]] <- selected$estimate[match(keep,selected$parameter)]
  }
  print(knitr::kable(tab,digits=4,
    caption="Duration-hazard recovery (annual hazards, not quarterly transition probabilities)"))
}
```

New outputs are under `four_wave_ar1/recovery_continuous_clock`; the failed
legacy checks remain under `four_wave_ar1/recovery`. The empirical continuation
defaults to a new `clock_joint1` label and rejects stale-source checkpoints.

# 12. Repaired four-wave AR(1): empirical Panel A refit

## Changes and scope

- Re-estimate all 33 parameters under the repaired continuous-clock likelihood
  on the same 316,889 Panel A records (101,916 collapsed likelihood cells).
- Start at the best converged pre-repair fit, preserve the old fit, and use a
  separate output label. Require optimizer convergence and an independent
  projected central score no greater than $10^{-5}$ per unit of sample weight.
- Keep the duration hazards, tenure reporting specification, fixed equal
  reliability-class shares, and free initial employment probability unchanged.
  Do not re-estimate the three-wave comparator or introduce AR(2) in this step.
- Compare quarterly entry and exit probabilities using the same pooled
  posterior-origin-risk and survey weights. Misclassification refers to
  employment-status error, not duration contamination.

```{r four-wave-clock-empirical, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
empirical_dir <- file.path(dirname(recovery_dir),"continuous_clock_empirical")
empirical_file <- file.path(empirical_dir,"comparison_latest.rds")
if (file.exists(empirical_file)) {
  empirical <- readRDS(empirical_file)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(empirical$best$converged),
    isTRUE(empirical$best$independent_score_pass))
  cmp <- empirical$comparison
  tab <- data.frame(Measure=c("Entry rate","Exit rate","Misclassification rate",
    "Initial employment"), `Pre-repair`=100*cmp$legacy,
    Repaired=100*cmp$repaired, `Change (pp)`=cmp$change_percentage_points,
    check.names=FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(tab,digits=3,
    caption="Panel A four-wave AR(1): main rates (percent)"))
  cat(sprintf("\nRepaired log likelihood: %.3f; maximum projected central score: %.3g.\n",
    empirical$best$loglik,empirical$best$gradient_max))
  cat(sprintf("\nRe-optimization improves the repaired objective by %.3f relative to the old parameter vector.\n",
    empirical$repaired_objective_gain))
} else cat("The empirical refit has not yet been consolidated; no revised rates are reported here.\n")
```

```{r four-wave-clock-empirical-hazards, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (file.exists(empirical_file)) {
  print(knitr::kable(empirical$hazards,digits=4,
    col.names=c("Hazard","Duration","Pre-repair","Repaired"),
    caption="Panel A duration coefficients: annual hazards"))
}
```

## Findings and interpretation

- The repaired empirical fit converges with optimizer code zero and a
  separately recomputed maximum projected central score of
  $5.53\times10^{-6}$. All 33 parameters were optimized from the best
  converged legacy starting vector. This is one empirical starting point,
  not a new dispersed-start exercise.
- Entry rises from 2.603% to 2.693% per quarter; exit rises from 4.060% to
  4.092%. Employment-status misclassification falls from 2.765% to 2.646%,
  and initial employment rises from 48.705% to 49.108%.
- Thus the repair changes the estimates modestly rather than overturning
  their main interpretation. Estimated status misclassification remains
  material, while exit probability conditional on employment remains above
  entry probability conditional on nonemployment. Those probabilities have
  different populations at risk and should not be directly subtracted to
  infer the change in employment.
- The largest duration-hazard adjustment is in the shortest nonemployment
  band: its annual entry hazard rises from about 0.509 to 0.563. Longer-duration
  entry hazards remain substantially lower; exit hazards change comparatively
  little. These are annual hazard coefficients, not the weighted quarterly
  entry probabilities in the main comparison.

The old likelihood is retained for historical auditing, not as a nested-model
benchmark: changing a defective probability construction means that its
difference from the repaired likelihood is not an LR statistic. The gain
reported above compares two parameter vectors under the *same repaired*
objective. Neither convergence nor the recovery checks establish strong
identification of the two reliability dispersions or a globally unique optimum.
No analytical or bootstrapped standard errors are estimated in this step.

At the new fitted parameter vector, the independent full-sample R evaluator
agrees with the compiled likelihood within $4.52\times10^{-8}$ and with its
posteriors within $1.24\times10^{-14}$. The repaired log likelihood is
-2,894,475.050, a gain of 414.246 over evaluating the old parameter vector
under the repaired law. The focused regression suite passes 249 checks.

Execution note: a trailing parsing error was reported after the optimizer,
independent score check, fit save, and rate printing had completed; the runner
had been edited while active. The current runner parses cleanly. A fresh
process loaded the saved fit and successfully performed the independent
full-sample checks and consolidation above. The error did not require a new
estimation or affect the saved parameter estimates.

Run `refine_four_wave_ar1_fast.R` with label `clock_joint1`, using
`fit_fast_start_plus_latest.rds` as the start, then run
`summarise_four_wave_clock_empirical.R`. The collector verifies the full-sample
R reference at the new parameters and stores rates, annual hazards, all
transformed coefficients, posteriors, convergence diagnostics, and source/input
fingerprints in `four_wave_ar1/continuous_clock_empirical`. These files do not
replace the legacy results or the separate simulation-recovery outputs.

# 13. Four-wave duration model with two AR(2) return effects

A compact candidate paper Table 9, including history-specific entry and exit
probabilities, is provided in `four_wave_duration_results.Rmd`. Rebuild its
LaTeX and unrounded CSV snapshot with
`scripts/build_four_wave_duration_paper_table.R`; this reads the saved fits
without re-estimation. Existing paper Tables 1--8 are unchanged. Analytical
uncertainty and the questionnaire-motivated sensitivity checks remain pending.

## Changes and identifying restrictions

- Add one entry and one exit coefficient to the repaired Panel A model;
  re-estimate all 35 parameters jointly. Keep duration-reporting mechanisms,
  duration reliability classes, and the estimation sample unchanged.
- For transitions 2-to-3 and 3-to-4, shift the log odds of a transition when
  the current latent state differs from the preceding latent state. Positive
  coefficients mean an increased probability of returning to the prior state.
- Retain free initial employment and the AR(1) law for transition 1-to-2.
  This is an explicit initial-pair restriction, not an assertion of stationarity
  or an estimate of unobserved pre-panel history. A free initial-pair model is
  deferred to a sensitivity check.
- Use forward numerical gradients during optimization and an independent
  central score for acceptance. Every accepted fit must have optimizer code
  zero and maximum projected central score at most $10^{-5}$. Use a main
  start and two perturbed starts, with all nuisance parameters free.

Writing $S_t=1$ for employment and $r_{01,t},r_{10,t}$ for the existing
duration-dependent AR(1) probabilities, for $t=2,3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}P(S_{t+1}=1\mid S_t=0,\ldots)
 &=\operatorname{logit}(r_{01,t})+b_N\,1\{S_{t-1}=1\},\\
\operatorname{logit}P(S_{t+1}=0\mid S_t=1,\ldots)
 &=\operatorname{logit}(r_{10,t})+b_E\,1\{S_{t-1}=0\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\exp(b_N)$ is the entry-odds multiplier after a recent exit and
$\exp(b_E)$ is the exit-odds multiplier after a recent entry, holding the
baseline duration-dependent probability fixed. These are **odds ratios, not
hazard ratios**. Apply them after the existing integration over category or
unobserved wrong-state durations. Do not alter the marginal duration-reporting
distributions or impose a new stationary duration distribution.

The implementation reuses the validated AR(1) likelihood through the exact
identity $L_2=L_1\sum_hP_1(h\mid\text{reports})P_2(h)/P_1(h)$. The AR(1)
likelihood and posterior are recomputed at every new nuisance vector: neither
is fixed during estimation. The independent R reference instead constructs
the AR(2) history prior directly before combining reporting probabilities.
Class and job-change posterior aggregates must also be recomputed under AR(2);
they cannot simply be copied from the AR(1) evaluator.

## Validation and recovery

Zero effects reproduce the full-sample repaired AR(1) likelihood and
posteriors. Nonzero effects agree with the independent direct-prior R
calculation. Four exhaustive finite-support joint-probability checks sum to
one, within the tenure-tail allowance. Three 10,000-person simulations check
all 35 likelihood scores at known nonzero coefficients. The largest pooled
absolute discrepancy is 2.18 Monte Carlo standard errors; the entry and exit
AR(2) discrepancies are 0.83 and -0.01. Twenty-four added unit checks cover nesting,
reference agreement, the seeded simulator, and which histories receive each
effect. These checks concern implementation, not precision of empirical effects.

```{r four-wave-ar2-recovery, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
ar2_dir <- file.path(dirname(dirname(recovery_dir)),"four_wave_ar2")
ar2_recovery_file <- file.path(ar2_dir,"recovery/recovery_latest.rds")
if (file.exists(ar2_recovery_file)) {
  ar2_recovery <- readRDS(ar2_recovery_file)
  print(knitr::kable(ar2_recovery$summary[c("replication","start","converged",
    "ar2_entry_truth","ar2_entry","ar2_exit_truth","ar2_exit")],digits=4,row.names=FALSE,
    caption="AR(2) recovery with all 35 parameters free: two 5,000-person samples"))
} else cat("The full-parameter recovery exercise has not yet been consolidated.\n")
```

## Empirical comparison

All three full-parameter recovery fits converge, with independent projected
central scores below $4.4\times10^{-6}$. The two starts on sample 1 differ by
less than 0.0004 likelihood units and 0.00024 in either AR(2) coefficient.
The generating entry coefficient is 1.099; estimates are 1.245 and 0.964
across the two samples. The generating exit coefficient is 0.693; estimates
are 0.472 and 0.620. These are encouraging implementation checks, not a
large-sample bias or coverage study. After projecting out all nuisance-score
directions in the 30,000-person score simulation, the two-by-two information
matrix has eigenvalues 70.78 and 56.65: the two return effects have separately
varying scores in this experiment.

```{r four-wave-ar2-empirical, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
ar2_file <- file.path(ar2_dir,"empirical/comparison_latest.rds")
if (file.exists(ar2_file)) {
  ar2_results <- readRDS(ar2_file)
  rows <- ar2_results$summary[match(c("AR1",ar2_results$best_label),ar2_results$summary$model),]
  labels <- c("Entry rate (%)","Exit rate (%)","Misclassification rate (%)",
    "Initial employment (%)","Log likelihood","N")
  column <- function(x) c(sprintf("%.3f",100*unlist(x[c("entry","exit","misclassification","initial_employment")])),
    formatC(x$loglik,format="f",digits=3,big.mark=","),format(x$n,big.mark=","))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=labels,AR1=column(rows[1,]),AR2=column(rows[2,])),
    row.names=FALSE,caption="Repaired four-wave duration model: AR(1) and AR(2), Panel A"))
  b <- unname(unlist(rows[2,c("ar2_entry","ar2_exit")]))
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Entry return effect (log odds)",
    "Exit return effect (log odds)","Entry return odds ratio","Exit return odds ratio"),
    AR1=c(0,0,1,1),AR2=c(b,exp(b))),digits=3,row.names=FALSE,
    caption="Return effects: both coefficients are fixed at zero in AR(1)"))
  cat(sprintf("\nLog-likelihood gain: %.3f; twice the gain: %.3f.\n",
    ar2_results$likelihood_gain,ar2_results$lr_statistic))
  print(knitr::kable(ar2_results$summary[-1,c("model","loglik","score","ar2_entry","ar2_exit")],
    digits=c(0,3,8,4,4),row.names=FALSE,caption="AR(2) starting-point and convergence checks"))
} else cat("No validated empirical AR(2) comparison has been consolidated yet.\n")
```

All main rates pool the three transitions using survey weights and posterior
origin-risk weights; only the last two transition probabilities contain an
AR(2) term. Initial employment is the estimated initial probability. The
misclassification parameter concerns employment status, not duration reports.
Unlike the historical pre-repair comparison, these two models are nested under
one repaired probability law. Any formal LR inference still requires regularity
and identification assumptions; the likelihood gain alone is not a validation
of causal state dependence.

```{r four-wave-ar2-implications, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (file.exists(ar2_file)) {
  for (direction in c("Entry","Exit")) {
    rows <- ar2_results$implications[ar2_results$implications$transition==direction,]
    measures <- c("raw_reversal","not_confirmed","genuine_reversed","genuine_persistent")
    tab <- data.frame(Measure=c("Raw reversal","Not confirmed","Genuine, reversed","Genuine, persistent"),
      AR1=100*as.numeric(rows[rows$model=="AR1",measures]),
      AR2=100*as.numeric(rows[rows$model=="AR2",measures]))
    table_tex <- knitr::kable(tab,format="latex",booktabs=TRUE,digits=2,longtable=FALSE,
      label=paste0("four-wave-ar2-",tolower(direction),"-implications"),
      caption=paste("Posterior decomposition of apparent",tolower(direction),"transitions (\\%)"))
    table_tex <- sub("\\begin{table}","\\begin{table}[H]",table_tex,fixed=TRUE)
    cat("\n```{=latex}\n",table_tex,"\n```\n",sep="")
  }
}
```

This decomposition pools transitions 1-to-2 and 2-to-3, which have an observed
follow-up wave. A transition is confirmed only when the latent origin and
destination match its apparent direction. The three model-based categories partition
apparent transitions into not confirmed, genuine but reversed next wave, and
genuine and persistent next wave. All four reports inform the posterior; this
is a retrospective decomposition, not a forecast using just two reports.
"Not confirmed" does not distinguish misreporting from record-matching errors.

```{r four-wave-ar2-hazards, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (file.exists(ar2_file)) print(knitr::kable(ar2_results$hazards,digits=4,
  caption="Baseline annual duration hazards: the AR(2) odds adjustment is additional"))
```

## Findings and interpretation

- All three empirical starts converge with independent projected central
  scores between $3.68\times10^{-6}$ and $7.70\times10^{-6}$. Their entry,
  exit, and status-misclassification rates differ by less than 0.00007
  percentage points, and their return coefficients by less than 0.00027.
  The highest-likelihood run is `plus`; its log likelihood exceeds repaired
  AR(1) by 2,196.404 (twice the gain is 4,392.807). The small likelihood
  spread across starts is 0.112, not evidence that every nuisance parameter
  is strongly identified or that a global optimum has been proved.
- The entry return coefficient is 1.299 and the exit return coefficient
  1.931: odds multipliers of 3.666 and 6.895, respectively. These duration
  controls do not absorb the tendency to return to the preceding state.
  Current-job tenure is not the same as uninterrupted employment duration
  when workers can change jobs while remaining employed; this is one reason
  surviving history effects need not contradict duration dependence.
- Average quarterly entry rises from 2.693% to 3.206%, and exit from 4.092%
  to 4.775%. Status misclassification falls modestly, from 2.646% to 2.441%;
  initial employment barely changes (49.108% versus 49.102%). The main
  interpretation is more genuine turnover, not a large revision to initial
  employment or the disappearance of misclassification.
- Among apparent entries, the share inferred to be genuine and reversed
  next wave rises from 6.48% to 13.99%; among apparent exits it rises from
  5.54% to 10.06%. Persistent-transition shares change much less. Nevertheless,
  55.80% of apparent entries and 45.88% of apparent exits are not confirmed
  in their reported direction under AR(2). The model therefore attributes
  more short-lived movement to genuine transitions while retaining an
  important role for misclassification, from either reporting or matching
  errors. These are shares of all apparent transitions, not a decomposition
  conditional on observing a reversal.
- After projecting out all 33 nuisance-score directions, the empirical
  two-effect information matrix has eigenvalues 1,226.75 and 1,634.83
  (condition number 1.33), unchanged across three projection tolerances.
  This supports local separation of the two return effects; it does not
  remove the earlier caveat about weak duration-reliability separation.
  No parameter reaches its numerical bound in the selected fit.

The full-sample direct-prior R and reweighted compiled likelihoods agree to
displayed machine precision; the maximum posterior difference is
$3.84\times10^{-15}$. Analytical return-coefficient scores agree with the
numerical scores within $4.3\times10^{-11}$. The weighted posterior mean status
misclassification is 2.44142%, consistent with the common fitted probability.
The focused suite passes 273 checks, including the audit table chunks.

## Remaining checks

- Check sensitivity to the initial-pair restriction before a structural
  interpretation. Keep broader reliability-mixture refinements secondary.
- Retain the separate caveat from Section 11: the timegap clock at a newly
  entered nonemployment spell is still drawn from the existing marginal law,
  rather than restricted to an onset within the last quarter. The AR(2)
  extension does not repair or validate that substantive modelling assumption.
- Interpret any surviving AR(2) effects as conditional associations, potentially
  reflecting residual duration misspecification, omitted heterogeneity, or
  reporting assumptions. No analytical or bootstrap standard errors are
  computed in this first extension.

Reproduce with `validate_four_wave_ar2.R`, `recover_four_wave_ar2.R`,
`estimate_four_wave_ar2.R`, and `summarise_four_wave_ar2.R`, in that order.
Outputs reside in the four-wave AR(2) results directory; repaired AR(1) and
historical pre-repair objects are preserved.

# 14. Subsequent extensions

The flexible baseline repairs the calendar distribution, exact retention and
local revisions capture part of the serial dependence, and separate
clock-specific reliability dispersions capture additional clustering of
duration irregularities. Following the decision to limit further work on
reliability-class separation, the remaining work should proceed in this order:

The repaired Panel A AR(1) refit is reported in Section 12. Its AR(2)
extension, recovery, nearby-start checks, local-identification diagnostic,
and first reversal comparison are completed in Section 13. The same-person
three-wave re-estimation remains omitted at the author's request.

1. check sensitivity to the initial-pair rule and the clean timegap
   distribution at a new nonemployment spell, changing one assumption at a time;
2. if a structural interpretation of the return effects is required, assess
   finer short-duration controls and remaining observed or unobserved
   heterogeneity rather than treating AR(2) coefficients as causal effects;
3. compute approximate analytical uncertainty once the preferred specification
   is settled, treating weak nuisance directions explicitly; and
4. retain uncertainty about reliability-class separation as a limitation.
   Additional class-share and bootstrap sensitivity work
   is secondary rather than a prerequisite for the employment extension.
